The two always go together, in opposite directions. You can't have the gamma without paying the theta, or collect the theta without taking the gamma. It is the fundamental trade-off of every options position.

docs.title: Where Theta hits hardest
docs.text: Maximum for ATM options (where time value is largest, the knife's edge). Low for a deep ITM option (its value is almost all intrinsic, so there's little time value to decay). Same place as maximum Gamma (ATM), which makes sense, they are two sides of the same coin.

docs.title: Decay isn't linear
docs.text: It accelerates as expiry approaches, especially for an ATM option. The last days of an ATM option's life are brutal, time value collapses.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text: Theta = the daily decay of the option's time value. Negative for the buyer, positive for the seller. Maximum ATM, accelerates near expiry. Always the mirror of gamma, the price you pay for convexity.

docs.title: 18. Vega
docs.text: Episode 18

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: Delta and Gamma were about the stock price, Theta about time. Vega is about volatility, the size of expected moves. We had come across volatility without covering it (Options episode, "the more volatile the stock, the more expensive the options", and the VIX).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Vega measures how much the option's price changes when the volatility of the underlying moves by 1 point (1%). Volatility = how much the market expects the stock to move around in all directions.

docs.title: Why volatility pushes the price up
docs.text: An option is a bet on a future move. The harder the stock moves, the higher the chance it crosses the strike and finishes profitable. So more volatility = a more expensive option, for a call and for a put (both benefit from a big move, each in its own direction).

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Call at €5, Vega = 0.20.

  • Volatility 20% → 21% (+1 point): option ~€5.20.
  • Volatility 20% → 18% (-2 points): option ~€4.60.

And this without the stock moving a single cent. It is only the market's expectation of the size of future moves that changes.

docs.title: Buyer vs seller
docs.text:
• Buyer: long vega, gains if volatility rises.
  • Seller: short vega, gains if volatility falls.

docs.title: Trading volatility, not direction (the core of the job)
docs.text: With Delta you bet on direction (up/down). With Vega you bet on the size of moves, with no view on direction. Example: an election or earnings in a week. You don't know if it will go up or down, but you are sure it will move a lot. Buying options (long vega) profits from the rise in volatility whatever the final direction. A pure bet on "something is going to happen".

docs.title: Implied vs realized volatility (key distinction)
docs.text: Vega reacts to implied volatility, the volatility the market expects (built into option prices today), not realized volatility (what actually happened in the past). An option's price can rise just because the market expects more turbulence, even if nothing has happened yet.

docs.title: The classic trap, the vol crush
docs.text: Just before a big event (quarterly earnings), implied volatility is inflated (everyone expects movement). Once the event has passed, the uncertainty disappears and implied volatility collapses (the "vol crush"). The trap: a beginner buys a call before earnings, the stock rises as hoped, but the option still loses value because the vega collapse ate more than the price rise brought in. Right on direction, but still a loss.

docs.title: Where Vega is strongest
docs.text: Maximum ATM and for long expiries (the more time left, the more room volatility has to act). Same place as max gamma and theta. They all measure the same "time value" from different angles.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text: Vega = the sensitivity of the option's price to volatility. Long vega (buyer) gains if vol rises, short vega (seller) gains if it falls. It lets you bet on the size of moves with no view on direction. Watch out for the vol crush after events.

docs.title: 19. Implied Volatility
docs.text: Episode 19

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: Vega measured sensitivity to volatility. But which volatility? Implied volatility, the one the market expects, built into option prices. It is what options traders actually trade. (Note: we skip Rho, sensitivity to interest rates. It is the least important Greek and is almost ignored on equity desks.)

docs.title: Definition (CFA-confirmed)
docs.text:
A model is just a formula that takes several known inputs, runs the calculation, and spits out a single number (here, the fair price of the option). The standard model is called Black-Scholes (or Black-Scholes-Merton, 1973).

So the price of an option comes out of this model, which takes as inputs the stock price, the strike, the time remaining, interest rates, and volatility. All of these inputs are known except future volatility.

(Nuance: pure Black-Scholes assumes a single, constant vol, which is wrong in practice. Hence the volatility skew (episode 21) and more advanced models like Heston, Dupire, SABR.)

Implied volatility is found by running the model in reverse: you observe the option's actual market price, and you look for the volatility you would need to plug into the model to get back to that price. Vol is the only unknown (everything else is observable).

Price observed in the market → inverted model → what volatility explains this price? = implied volatility

docs.title: What it represents
docs.text:
The market's expectation of how big future moves will be, as built into option prices right now. High IV = expensive options, the market expects a big move. Low IV = cheap options, the market expects calm.

Rigorous nuance. IV is a risk-neutral measure, not a pure forecast. It is not exactly "what the market thinks vol will be".

docs.title: IV almost always runs higher than realized (variance risk premium)
docs.text:
This is the point that separates reciting from understanding. IV systematically overestimates actual moves. This is the variance risk premium (VRP). People pay a premium for protection (institutions buying puts) and for the risk of a sudden jump, so option prices carry a premium above the move that is actually expected.

Figures as of 12 March 2026 on SPY: 30-day IV at 25.74% vs realized volatility at 16.68%, a gap of ~9 points. Positive ~79% of the time. Selling this gap is a strategy in its own right. [source SharpeTwo]

docs.title: Implied vs realized
docs.text:
• Implied: the vol the market expects, extracted from option prices today. This is what Vega reacts to.
  • Realized: the vol that actually happened, measured after the fact on past moves.

docs.title: Quoting in vol (desk/dealer convention, NOT retail)
docs.text:
On a desk or between dealers, options are not quoted in euros but in vol. A dealer says "I'll buy at 18 vol", not "at 5 euros". The euro price is just the output calculated after plugging that vol into the model. What is really being negotiated is volatility.

To frame carefully. This is the convention of the OTC / institutional world. Retail traders see premiums in dollars on their broker (with IV shown next to them). Do NOT say "the € price doesn't exist" (wrong, it settles in cash). Say "they think in vol".

docs.title: Why it is central
docs.text: It is the real currency of options. A trader compares the quoted IV with their own vol forecast to spot mispriced options (IV > their forecast = expensive option to sell, IV < their forecast = cheap option to buy).

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text: Implied volatility = the vol extracted from the market price by inverting the model. It is the market's (risk-neutral) expectation of future moves, it almost always runs higher than realized (variance risk premium), and desks actually trade options in vol, not in price.

docs.title: 20. The Gamma Squeeze
docs.text: Episode 20

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: A synthesis of several episodes: gamma, delta hedging, market makers, and the GameStop short squeeze. A concrete case where option hedging sends a stock price through the roof.

docs.title: The setup
docs.text: When you buy a call, someone sells it to you, usually a market maker. They don't want to bet on direction, just collect their spread. So they hedge: having sold a call, they buy some of the stock to stay delta-neutral.

docs.title: The key mechanism, gamma
docs.text: The number of shares they need to hold is not fixed. When the stock rises, the call they sold becomes more sensitive to the stock (its delta goes up), so they have to buy even more shares to stay hedged. That is gamma (episode 16).

docs.title: The self-feeding loop
docs.text:
• A crowd buys calls on a stock in huge size.
  • The market makers selling them buy shares to hedge.
  • That buying pushes the stock up.
  • Higher stock = they need even more shares, so they buy again.
  • Which pushes the stock up further.

The loop feeds itself, and the price goes vertical in a few days, driven by hedging, not by any real revaluation of the company.

docs.title: Gamma squeeze vs short squeeze (key distinction)
docs.text:
• Short squeeze (episode 12): short sellers forced to buy back the stock to close their positions.
  • Gamma squeeze: market makers forced to buy the stock to hedge options they sold.

Different people, different reason. GameStop 2021 was both at the same time, which explains the size of the move.

docs.title: The counterintuitive point
docs.text: Nobody in the loop is trying to push the price up. The market makers would rather not buy at all. They are forced to, again and again, by their own hedging.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text: Gamma squeeze = a loop where massive call buying forces market makers to buy the stock to hedge, which pushes the price up, which forces them to buy even more. It is delta hedging + gamma spiraling out of control. Not to be confused with a short squeeze, even though the two can combine.

docs.title: 21. The Volatility Skew
docs.text: Episode 21

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: A direct follow-up to implied vol (episode 19). Black-Scholes assumes a single, constant vol, which is wrong in practice, and the skew is the visual proof of that flaw. A classic S&T interview question.

docs.title: The starting point, a wrong assumption
docs.text: Each option has its own implied vol (extracted from its price). A stock has lots of strikes, so lots of implied vols. Black-Scholes assumes volatility is a property of the stock itself, a single level of agitation. The strike is just a number chosen in the contract, with no effect on how much the stock actually moves. So in theory, all options with the same expiry should give the same implied vol. A flat line.

docs.title: What we actually see
docs.text:
It is not flat. If you plot implied vol against strike, you get a curve. Low strikes have a much higher implied vol than high strikes.

Example, Apple at 100, 1-month expiry.

  • Strike 80: 32%
  • Strike 100 (ATM): 20%
  • Strike 120: 18%

docs.title: Why the curve slopes (the core)
docs.text:
1. Fear of crashes. Stocks fall more violently than they rise. The market prices a bigger downside risk.
  2. Hedging demand. Everyone buys low-strike puts to protect themselves. This strong demand pushes up the price of those puts, and a higher option price = a higher implied vol (we invert the model). Fear turns mechanically into inflated vol on low strikes.

docs.title: The two shapes
docs.text:
• Skew (or smirk): a sloping curve, high vol on the left (low strikes), low on the right. This is what you see on equities and indices.
  • Smile: both edges curve up, a symmetric shape. More common in FX and commodities.

docs.title: Put or call? Parity settles it (link to episode 14)
docs.text: At each strike there are both, a call AND a put. Put-Call Parity forces them to have exactly the same implied vol. So a point on the curve is neither a call nor a put, it is a single number shared by both. "Puts on the left / calls on the right" just means we read the vol off the OTM (liquid) option at each end.

docs.title: The mathematical proof (for revision)
docs.text:
Parity (pure arbitrage, no model assumption): C − P = S − K·e^(−rT). Black-Scholes prices respect it for any σ: BS_call(σ) − BS_put(σ) = S − K·e^(−rT).

Let σ_c be the call's implied vol (BS_call(σ_c) = C_mkt). Plugging σ_c into BS parity:

BS_put(σ_c) = BS_call(σ_c) − (S − K·e^(−rT))
            = C_mkt − (S − K·e^(−rT))
            = C_mkt − (C_mkt − P_mkt)   [market parity]
            = P_mkt

So σ_c is also the put's implied vol. Since implied vol is unique (Vega = ∂C/∂σ = S·√T·N'(d1) > 0, so BS is strictly increasing in σ), we get σ_p = σ_c.

docs.title: Black-Scholes formula (reminder, where vol lives)
docs.text:
C = S·N(d1) − K·e^(−rT)·N(d2)
d1 = [ ln(S/K) + (r + σ²/2)·T ] / (σ·√T)
d2 = d1 − σ·√T

The only unknown input is σ. The skew is the fact that σ_impl(K) depends on K instead of being constant, direct proof that the constant-vol assumption is wrong.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text: The skew = implied vol plotted against strike is not flat but sloping (equities) or smile-shaped (FX). It is caused by fear of crashes and hedging demand, which inflate the vol of low-strike puts. Each point is shared by the call and the put at that strike (parity). It is the empirical proof that Black-Scholes (constant vol) is wrong.

docs.title: 22. The Straddle
docs.text: Episode 22

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: The strategy that brings all the Greeks together at once (delta, gamma, vega, theta). It makes the whole options arc concrete.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Buy a call AND a put, same strike, same expiry. You pay both premiums. It is a bet on a big move, whatever the direction. If the stock moves hard enough one way or the other, one of the two sides pays off big.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Apple at €100. Call strike 100 (premium €4) + put strike 100 (premium €4). Total cost = €8.

  • Apple at 120: call worth 20, put 0 → 20 − 8 = +€12
  • Apple at 80: put worth 20, call 0 → 20 − 8 = +€12
  • Apple at 100 (right at the strike): both at 0 → −€8 (max loss)
  • Apple at 105: call worth 5, put 0 → 5 − 8 = −€3 (it moved, but not enough)

docs.title: Breakevens
docs.text: You only make money if the move exceeds the total cost (€8). Upper breakeven = 100 + 8 = €108. Lower breakeven = 100 − 8 = €92. In between, you lose. It is not "I bet it moves", it is "I bet it moves by more than €8".

docs.title: The Greeks, all at once
docs.text:
• Delta neutral (at the start). Call +0.5, put −0.5, they cancel out → no bet on direction. Nuance: only true at entry. As soon as the stock moves, gamma tilts delta in the direction of the move (e.g. Apple at 110 → call delta +0.8, put −0.2, total +0.6, net long).
  • Long gamma. You love big moves, in both directions, and gains accelerate when the stock takes off.
  • Long vega. If implied volatility rises, both options gain value, even before the stock moves.
  • Short theta (negative theta). Every quiet day is expensive, you pay the decay on TWO options at once.

docs.title: The trap, vol crush
docs.text: A straddle is most tempting before an event (earnings, an election), when a big move is expected. But that is exactly when implied vol is inflated, so both premiums are expensive. The actual move has to beat what is already priced in. After the event, vol crush drives the value down (long vega hurts). You can see the stock move as expected and still lose if the move is smaller than what was anticipated.

docs.title: The seller (short straddle)
docs.text: The exact opposite: collects both premiums and wants the stock to stay still. Short gamma, short vega, positive theta. Very dangerous, it loses if the stock moves hard in either direction.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text: Long straddle = call + put at the same strike. Delta neutral (at the start), long gamma, long vega, short theta. A pure bet on the size of the move, not the direction. It wins on a big move OR a rise in vol, and loses if the stock stalls. Watch out for vol crush after events.

docs.title: 23. The Strangle
docs.text: Episode 23

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: The straddle's direct cousin (episode 22), and the comparison everyone asks about right after.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Same setup as a straddle: you buy a call and a put, same expiry. The difference is that the two strikes are different, and both are out of the money (OTM), one below the current price and one above.

docs.title: Why do this instead of a straddle
docs.text: OTM options cost less than ATM options (see the Delta and moneyness episode). So the strangle is cheaper to enter than the straddle.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Apple at 100.

Setup Cost Straddle call 100 + put 100 8 Strangle call 110 (premium 2) + put 90 (premium 2) 4

Half the price.

docs.title: Breakevens, the real trade-off
docs.text:
Upper breakeven Lower breakeven Straddle 108 92 Strangle 114 86

The strangle paid less, so it needs a bigger move to become profitable. The straddle makes money as soon as Apple goes above 108 or below 92. The strangle needs 114 or 86.

Strangle math: upper breakeven = call strike + total cost = 110 + 4 = 114. Lower breakeven = put strike − total cost = 90 − 4 = 86.

docs.title: The Greeks
docs.text:
Same profile as the straddle at entry: delta neutral, long gamma, long vega, short theta. The difference comes down to two things only:

  • how much you pay for that exposure (less)
  • how far the stock has to go before it matters (further)

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text: The real choice is not straddle versus strangle in the abstract. It is: how big a move do you actually expect, and is it better to pay more upfront for a lower profitability bar (straddle), or pay less but need a bigger move (strangle).

docs.title: 24. The Vertical Spread
docs.text: Episode 24

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: Straddles and strangles are non-directional bets on the size of the move. The vertical spread is the opposite: a directional bet, built to cost less and risk less than a call or a put bought on its own.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Same expiry, same option type (two calls or two puts), two different strikes. You buy one and sell another. The premium collected on the option you sell reduces the cost, but the maximum gain becomes capped.

docs.title: The four versions
docs.text:
Calls Puts Bullish Bull call spread (you pay upfront) Bull put spread (you collect upfront) Bearish Bear call spread (you collect upfront) Bear put spread (you pay upfront)

"Bull" or "bear" = the direction you are betting on. Paying or collecting upfront = the direction of cash at entry. Paying upfront is called a debit spread, collecting is a credit spread.

docs.title: Bull call spread, step by step
docs.text:
Apple at 100. You buy the 100 call for 5 and sell the 110 call for 2.

  • Net cost: 5 − 2 = 3
  • Max loss: 3 (the whole cost)
  • Max gain: gap between strikes (10) − cost (3) = 7
  • Breakeven: 100 + 3 = 103

At expiry:

Apple ends at 100 call bought 110 call sold Net after the cost of 3 95 0 0 −3 103 3 0 0 110 10 0 +7 130 30 −20 +7

Above 110, the sold call loses exactly what the bought call gains on every extra euro. The gain stops growing at 7. That is the price of the cheaper entry.

docs.title: Why the sold call has no unlimited risk here
docs.text: Options episode: a call sold on its own ("naked") has unlimited loss, because you may have to buy the stock at the market price to deliver it. Here it is not naked. You also own the 100 call, which gives you the right to buy at 100. If Apple rises to 300 and you have to sell at 110, the 100 call lets you buy at 100 to deliver. The loss on the sold leg is covered by the gain on the bought leg. Hence a max loss limited to the 3 you paid.

docs.title: Comparison with the 100 call bought alone
docs.text:
100 call alone Bull call spread Cost 5 3 Max loss 5 3 Max gain unlimited 7 Breakeven 105 103

Cheaper, less risk, profitable sooner. In exchange, you give up all the gain above 110. If you expect a moderate rise (toward 110), the spread is the better choice. If you expect a very big move, the call alone is better.

docs.title: The Greeks
docs.text:
The sold option offsets part of the bought option, so everything is dampened (illustrative figures):

100 call bought 110 call sold Net Delta +0.50 −0.30 +0.20 Theta (per day) −0.07 +0.05 −0.02 Vega +0.20 −0.15 +0.05
  • Smaller delta: less exposed to direction than a call alone.
  • Theta close to zero: time hurts much less than with a call alone.
  • Low vega: a vol crush hurts much less, a good answer to the trap seen in the Straddle episode.

docs.title: Credit spreads, the mirror image
docs.text:
Bull put spread: you sell the 100 put for 5, buy the 90 put for 2, and collect 3 upfront.

  • Max gain: the 3 collected (if Apple stays above 100)
  • Max loss: gap (10) − credit (3) = 7 (if Apple falls below 90)
  • Breakeven: 100 − 3 = 97

You get paid first, and take a capped risk if you are wrong.

Bear put spread (the bearish debit counterpart): buy the 100 put, sell the 90 put. It makes money if the stock falls, with the gain capped below 90.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text: Vertical spread = buy one option and sell another of the same type, same expiry, different strike. Cheaper and less risky than a single option, with a capped gain. Dampened Greeks (smaller delta, theta, vega). Debit spread if you pay upfront, credit spread if you collect.

docs.title: 25. Black-Scholes
docs.text: Episode 25

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: Black-Scholes shows up in almost every options episode. Delta comes from it, implied volatility is what you get by running it backwards, and the skew exists because one of its assumptions is wrong. We never opened it up. This episode closes the options arc by explaining the model itself, where it comes from, how to price an option by hand, and why desks still use it when everyone knows it is wrong.

docs.title: What a model is
docs.text:
A model is a simplified version of reality written as a formula. You give it inputs, it gives you a number. It makes assumptions so the maths becomes possible, and those assumptions are never perfectly true. A good model is not an exact model. It is a model whose errors you know.

Black-Scholes takes 5 inputs and gives the "fair" price of a European option (one that can only be exercised at expiry).

docs.title: The problem before 1973
docs.text:
Before Black-Scholes, pricing a call meant guessing two things. Where the stock would end up, and what rate to use to discount a risky payoff. Everyone had their own estimate of the stock's return and their own appetite for risk, so everyone had their own price. There was no reference price.

What Black, Scholes and Merton showed is that you need neither the expected return nor the risk appetite. The price comes out of an arbitrage argument, just like put-call parity.

docs.title: The 5 inputs
docs.text:
Input Symbol What it is Where you find it Underlying price S The stock price today On the screen Strike K The exercise price written in the contract In the contract Maturity T Time left until expiry, in years (6 months = 0.5) In the contract Risk-free rate r What a riskless loan pays (government rate), continuously compounded On the screen Volatility σ (sigma) How much the stock moves around, in % per year Nobody knows it

Four of the five inputs are observable. The only one you have to estimate is volatility. That is why the whole options market revolves around vol, and why traders quote in vol rather than in dollars or euros.

What is not on the list matters just as much. There is no expected return for the stock, and no view from the trader on direction.

docs.title: The core idea, copying the option
docs.text: You can build an exact copy of an option with only two ingredients, shares and cash (borrowed or lent). If the copy pays exactly the same as the option in every scenario, the two must cost the same. Otherwise you buy the cheaper one, sell the more expensive one, and lock in a risk-free profit. This is the law of one price.

docs.title: A simple one-period version
docs.text:
To see the mechanism, simplify as much as possible. Stock at €100, in one year it is worth either €120 or €80. Interest rate 0%. Call with a €100 strike.

  • If the stock goes to €120, the call pays €20.
  • If it falls to €80, the call pays €0.

How many shares do you need to reproduce that? The call's payoff moves by €20, the stock's price moves by €40. So you need 20 / 40 = 0.5 shares. That 0.5 is the delta.

  • 0.5 shares are worth €60 if the stock goes up, €40 if it goes down.
  • You borrow €40 today (and pay back €40, since the rate is zero).
  • In the up scenario, 60 − 40 = €20. In the down scenario, 40 − 40 = €0.

The copy pays exactly like the call. Today it costs 0.5 × 100 − 40 = €10. So the call is worth €10.

We never used the probability that the stock goes up. Whether you think it has a 90% chance of rising or 10%, the call is worth €10. If someone sells it at €12, you sell it too, buy the copy at €10, and keep €2 whatever happens.

docs.title: Moving to the real model
docs.text: In reality the price does not take two values, it moves continuously. Black-Scholes does the same thing by cutting time into infinitely small steps. At every instant you adjust the number of shares you hold (this is delta hedging), and the copy tracks the option all the time. The formula is what you get when you push this reasoning to the limit.

docs.title: Why the expected return disappears
docs.text:
Because the price comes from a copy, it is the same for an optimistic investor, a pessimistic one, a careful one or a gambler. So you can do the maths in an imaginary world where everyone is risk-neutral and every stock earns, on average, the risk-free rate r. This is called risk-neutral pricing. It is not a claim about real life. It is a calculation shortcut that gives the right price because the copying argument guarantees it.

In practice this means the probabilities that come out of Black-Scholes (like N(d2)) are probabilities in that risk-neutral world, not real-world probabilities. On a desk people say "risk-neutral probability".

docs.title: The formula
docs.text:
For a European call on a stock that pays no dividend:

C = S × N(d1) − K × e^(−rT) × N(d2)

d1 = [ ln(S / K) + (r + σ² / 2) × T ] / ( σ × √T )
d2 = d1 − σ × √T

For a European put:

P = K × e^(−rT) × N(−d2) − S × N(−d1)

docs.title: Every symbol
docs.text:
• C and P, the price of the call and the put.
  • e, a mathematical constant worth about 2.718.
  • e^(−rT), the discount factor. It turns an amount paid at expiry into what it is worth today. At r = 4% and T = 1 year it equals 0.9608. So €100 in a year is worth €96.08 today.
  • ln, the natural logarithm. ln(S / K) measures the gap between the stock price and the strike as a (continuous) percentage. ln(1) = 0, so at the money (S = K) this term is zero. ln(110 / 100) ≈ 0.095, so about +9.5%.
  • √T, the square root of the maturity. Volatility grows with the square root of time, not with time. Over 4 years a stock moves roughly 2 times more than over 1 year, not 4 times more.
  • σ × √T, the total volatility over the whole life of the option.
  • N(x), a probability between 0 and 1, explained just below.

docs.title: N(x) and the bell curve
docs.text:
Picture a bell curve (the normal distribution). Most values sit close to 0, extreme values are rare. N(x) is the share of the bell curve that sits to the left of x.

x N(x) Reading −2 0.023 Almost nothing to the left −1 0.159 0 0.500 Exactly half 0.1 0.540 0.3 0.618 1 0.841 2 0.977 Almost everything to the left

Useful property, N(−x) = 1 − N(x). The bell curve is symmetric.

Black-Scholes assumes the logarithm of the price follows this normal distribution, so the price itself follows a log-normal distribution. In plain words, the price can never go negative, and a +50% move is roughly as likely as a −33% move (both are the same distance in log terms).

docs.title: d1 and d2
docs.text:
d1 and d2 measure how far in or out of the money the option is, in number of standard deviations (of "total vols"). The bigger they are, the deeper in the money the option is.

  • N(d2) = the (risk-neutral) probability that the call finishes in the money, so that you actually pay the strike.
  • N(d1) = the call's delta. It is the number of shares to hold in the copy. It is not exactly a probability, it is the sensitivity of the price to the stock (see episode 15).

d1 is always bigger than d2, and the gap between them is σ√T. That is why a call's delta is always a bit bigger than its probability of finishing in the money.

docs.title: Reading the formula in words
docs.text:
C = (what you get in stock, weighted) − (what you pay at the strike, weighted)
  • S × N(d1) = the value of the stock part of the copy. You hold N(d1) shares worth S each.
  • K × e^(−rT) × N(d2) = the cash borrowed in the copy. It is the discounted strike, multiplied by the probability of having to pay it.

This is exactly the structure of the one-period example (0.5 shares minus €40 borrowed), with values computed continuously.

docs.title: Worked example, step by step
docs.text:
Stock at €100, strike €100 (at the money), 1 year, rate 4%, vol 20%.

Step 1, d1.

ln(100 / 100) = 0
(r + σ² / 2) × T = (0.04 + 0.02) × 1 = 0.06
σ × √T = 0.20 × 1 = 0.20
d1 = (0 + 0.06) / 0.20 = 0.30

Step 2, d2.

d2 = 0.30 − 0.20 = 0.10

Step 3, the probabilities.

N(0.30) = 0.6179    (delta)
N(0.10) = 0.5398    (risk-neutral probability of finishing ITM)

Step 4, the discount factor.

e^(−0.04 × 1) = 0.9608

Step 5, the price.

C = 100 × 0.6179 − 100 × 0.9608 × 0.5398
C = 61.79 − 51.87
C = €9.93

The put, same inputs.

P = 100 × 0.9608 × N(−0.10) − 100 × N(−0.30)
P = 96.08 × 0.4602 − 100 × 0.3821
P = 44.21 − 38.21
P = €6.00

Check with put-call parity. C − P = S − K × e^(−rT), so 9.93 − 6.00 = 3.93 and 100 − 96.08 = 3.92. It matches (the gap is rounding). Black-Scholes respects parity by construction.

Why is the call worth more than the put when both are at the money? Because the strike is paid in a year. With a positive rate, paying €100 later costs less than paying €100 today, which helps the call buyer. At a zero rate, the at-the-money call and put are worth exactly the same (€7.97 each in this example).

docs.title: What moves the price
docs.text:
Same base option (S = 100, K = 100, T = 1 year, r = 4%, σ = 20%), changing one input at a time.

What changes Call Put What to take from it Base case €9.93 €6.00 Vol at 30% €13.75 €9.83 More vol = both more expensive Vol at 10% €6.18 €2.26 Less vol = both cheaper Vol at 21% (+1 point) €10.31 €6.39 +€0.38, that is vega Stock at €101 €10.55 €5.63 Call +€0.63, close to the 0.62 delta Strike at €110 (OTM call) €5.66 €11.35 Strike at €90 (ITM call) €16.06 €2.53 3 months to expiry €4.49 €3.49 Less time = cheaper 1 month to expiry €2.47 €2.14 Rate at 0% €7.97 €7.97 Call = put at the money

Two things to see in this table.

  1. Vol is the input that matters most. Going from 20% to 30% lifts the call by almost 40%, without the stock or the date moving.
  2. Time does not work linearly. 3 months are worth €4.49, not a quarter of €9.93. That is the square root of time, and it is what makes theta speed up near expiry.

docs.title: The desk shortcut
docs.text:
For an at-the-money option with a low rate:

Call ≈ Put ≈ 0.4 × S × σ × √T

In the example, 0.4 × 100 × 0.20 × 1 = €8. The true price at a zero rate is €7.97. The 0.4 comes from 1 / √(2π) ≈ 0.399. It lets you price a straddle in your head (2 × 0.4 × S × σ × √T ≈ 0.8 × S × σ × √T) and read an option price as an expected move. That is the maths behind episode 22 on the straddle.

docs.title: The Greeks come out of the formula
docs.text:
Each Greek is the derivative of the Black-Scholes price with respect to one input. Write n(x) for the height of the bell curve at x, n(x) = e^(−x²/2) / √(2π).

Greek Formula (call) Value in the example Reading Delta N(d1) 0.618 +€0.62 if the stock gains €1 Gamma n(d1) / (S × σ × √T) 0.019 Delta gains 0.019 per €1 rise Vega S × n(d1) × √T (÷ 100 per vol point) €0.38 +€0.38 per vol point Theta −S × n(d1) × σ / (2√T) − r × K × e^(−rT) × N(d2) (÷ 365) −€0.016 per day The option loses 1.6 cents a day Rho K × T × e^(−rT) × N(d2) (÷ 100) €0.52 +€0.52 if rates rise by 1 point

The put's delta is N(d1) − 1 = −0.382. Gamma and vega are identical for a call and a put with the same strike and expiry, which follows from parity.

docs.title: Running it backwards, implied vol
docs.text:
In real life you do not know σ, but you can see the option's price on the screen. So you run the formula backwards. You look for the vol that, plugged into Black-Scholes, gives back the observed price. That is implied volatility.

If the at-the-money call in the example trades at €10.31 instead of €9.93, the implied vol is 21%. There is no closed-form formula for this reverse calculation, you solve it by trial and error (the price always rises with vol, so there is only one answer).

This is where Black-Scholes changes job. It is no longer used to find a price, it is used to translate a price into a vol. Options with different strikes and maturities become comparable on a single unit.

docs.title: The assumptions and where they break
docs.text: Assumption In reality Consequence Constant volatility Vol changes all the time and depends on the strike The skew and the smile No jumps, the price moves continuously Crashes, earnings announcements, gaps at the open Deep OTM puts are worth more than the model says Log-normal returns Tails are fatter, big moves happen more often Same effect, extremes are underpriced Continuous hedging with no costs You hedge at intervals, with fees and a bid-ask spread The hedge is never perfect, hedging P&L moves around Constant risk-free rate, borrow and lend at the same rate Rates move, borrowing costs more than lending Small effect on short options, bigger on long ones No dividends Many stocks pay dividends Merton's extension, you subtract the dividend yield Exercise only at expiry (European) US single-stock options are usually American You need binomial trees or other methods

docs.title: The 1987 crash
docs.text: Before October 1987, implied vol was roughly the same for every strike, as the model predicts. On 19 October 1987 the S&P 500 lost about 20% in a single day. Under a log-normal distribution with the vols of the time, that move was supposed to almost never happen. Since then the market charges more for OTM puts, and the skew has been a permanent feature of equity indices.

docs.title: How desks still use it
docs.text:
Nobody on a desk believes vol is constant. But everyone uses Black-Scholes as a quoting convention. You use a different vol for each strike and each maturity, which gives a volatility surface. The formula is still wrong, but by plugging the right vol into it for each option, you get back the market prices. A well-known line in the industry sums it up, roughly, you put the wrong number into the wrong formula to get the right price.

For exotic products, desks use richer models (local vol, stochastic vol like Heston, jump models), but those are calibrated to match the Black-Scholes prices of plain options.

docs.title: The rates cousins of Black-Scholes
docs.text:
On a rates desk you mostly see two variants.

  • Black 76, adapted by Fischer Black in 1976 for options on futures and forwards. It is the standard model for caps, floors and swaptions. You replace S with the forward rate.
  • Bachelier (the normal model), where the underlying moves in basis points rather than in percent. When European rates went below zero, Black 76 stopped working (you cannot take the log of a negative number). The swaption market moved to quoting in normal vol, in basis points per year.

This links directly to the swaps and yield curve episodes.

docs.title: A bit of history
docs.text:
• 1973. Fischer Black and Myron Scholes publish "The Pricing of Options and Corporate Liabilities" in the Journal of Political Economy. Robert Merton publishes a paper the same year that formalises the proof. The same year, the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE) opens, the first organised exchange for listed options. Traders adopt the formula very quickly.
  • 1987. The crash exposes the limits of the constant-vol assumption. The skew is born.
  • 1995. Fischer Black dies.
  • 1997. Scholes and Merton receive the Nobel prize in economics. The Nobel is not awarded posthumously, but the committee mentions Black's role.
  • 1998. Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM), the hedge fund where Scholes and Merton were partners, loses about $4.6 billion in a few months. The New York Fed organises a rescue by a group of banks. The collapse came mostly from huge leverage and bets on spreads converging, not from the option formula itself.

docs.title: Classic pitfalls
docs.text:
• Units. σ as an annual decimal (20% = 0.20), T in years (3 months = 0.25, 30 days ≈ 30 / 365). Putting T in days or σ in percent gives absurd prices.
  • Continuous rate. The formula uses a continuously compounded rate. A 4% annual rate is a continuous rate of ln(1.04) ≈ 3.92%. Small effect, but real.
  • N(d2) is not the real probability. It is a risk-neutral probability. It says nothing about what will actually happen.
  • N(d1) is not a probability. It is the delta. People sometimes use it as a rough proxy for the probability of finishing ITM, but in the model that role belongs to N(d2).
  • Historical vs implied vol. Plugging historical vol into the formula gives a "theoretical" price. The market quotes with implied vol. The two are almost always different (see the variance risk premium in episode 19).
  • American options and dividends. The basic formula only works for a European option with no dividend. An American call on a non-dividend stock is worth the same as a European one (early exercise is never worth it), but that is not true for an American put.
  • "The model is wrong so it is useless." Wrong. It is wrong, but it is the common language of the market. Everyone knows how to turn a price into a vol with the same formula.

docs.title: The S&T interview angle
docs.text:
"Walk me through Black-Scholes." The price of a European option depends on 5 inputs, stock price, strike, maturity, rate and vol. You can replicate the option with the stock and cash by adjusting the delta continuously, so by no-arbitrage the option is worth what the copy costs. The expected return does not appear. The formula is C = S N(d1) − K e^(−rT) N(d2), where N(d1) is the delta and N(d2) the risk-neutral probability of exercise.

"Which input matters most?" Vol, because it is the only one you cannot observe. The rest you read on the screen.

"Why doesn't the stock's expected return matter?" Because the price comes from replication. Two people who disagree on direction still have to agree on the price, otherwise one of them can arbitrage it.

"What are the model's limits?" Constant vol (contradicted by the skew), no jumps, tails too thin, continuous costless hedging. In practice the formula is kept as a convention and used with a vol surface.

"Roughly what is a 1-year at-the-money call worth, stock at 100, vol at 20%?" 0.4 × 100 × 0.20 ≈ 8. A bit more with positive rates (9.93 at 4%).

"Which model for a swaption?" Black 76 historically, Bachelier (normal vol) since negative rates.

docs.title: Links to previous episodes
docs.text:
• Options for the definitions of call, put, strike and premium.
  • Put-Call Parity, the same arbitrage reasoning, and a relationship Black-Scholes respects automatically.
  • Delta, Gamma, Theta, Vega, the derivatives of the formula.
  • Implied Volatility, the formula run backwards.
  • The Volatility Skew, the proof that the constant-vol assumption is wrong.
  • The Straddle, the 0.8 × S × σ × √T shortcut in practice.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text:
• Black-Scholes gives the price of a European option from 5 inputs, stock price, strike, maturity, rate and vol.
  • The core idea, you can copy the option with the stock and cash, so the option is worth what the copy costs. The expected return and any view on direction play no part.
  • C = S × N(d1) − K × e^(−rT) × N(d2). N(d1) is the delta, N(d2) the risk-neutral probability of finishing in the money.
  • Vol is the only unknown input, hence quoting in vol and implied vol.
  • At-the-money shortcut, price ≈ 0.4 × S × σ × √T.
  • The model is wrong (constant vol, no jumps) and the skew proves it. Desks still use it as a common language, with a different vol for each strike and maturity.

docs.title: 26. The Policy Rate
docs.text: Episode 26

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: Every rates episode in the series starts from the same point without ever explaining it. The yield curve starts at the overnight rate, the floating leg of a swap resets on an overnight rate, and repo produces SOFR. All of these rates are anchored by one decision, the central bank's policy rate. This episode explains what a central bank is, how it sets that rate without ever telling a bank what rate to charge, how the rate spreads to the rest of the economy, and why it gets raised or cut.

docs.title: What a central bank is
docs.text:
It is the bank of the banks. Commercial banks (BNP, JPMorgan, Deutsche Bank...) hold an account at the central bank. The money in those accounts is called reserves. Banks use reserves to pay each other at the end of every day. When you send money from your bank to someone at another bank, at the end of the chain it is reserves that move from one account to another at the central bank.

Key point, only the central bank can create reserves. Banks can lend reserves to each other, but they cannot make new ones. That monopoly is what lets the central bank control the price of very short-term money.

The main central banks.

Central bank Area Deciding committee Meetings Federal Reserve (Fed) United States FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) 8 a year European Central Bank (ECB) Euro area Governing Council 8 monetary policy meetings a year Bank of England (BoE) United Kingdom Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) 8 a year Bank of Japan (BoJ) Japan Policy Board 8 a year

docs.title: What the policy rate is
docs.text:
It is the rate the central bank uses to steer the price of overnight money, meaning money lent from today to tomorrow. Each central bank has its own.

  • Fed. A target range for the fed funds rate, 0.25% wide. For example 4.25% to 4.50%. The fed funds rate is the rate at which banks lend reserves to each other overnight, unsecured.
  • ECB. Three rates, of which only one really matters today, the deposit facility rate (DFR).
  • BoE. Bank Rate, a single rate.

When people say "the Fed hiked by 25 bps", it means the whole range moved up by 0.25% (1 bp, a basis point, is 0.01%).

docs.title: The mechanism, a floor and a ceiling
docs.text:
The central bank does not call anyone to impose a rate. It sets two rates, and the market settles between them.

  • The floor. The rate the central bank pays banks on money left with it. No bank will lend to another bank below that, because leaving the money at the central bank earns that rate with zero risk.
  • The ceiling. The rate at which the central bank lends to banks against securities pledged as collateral. No bank will borrow from another bank above that, because it can borrow from the central bank directly.

docs.title: Worked example, the ECB
docs.text:
Take ECB rates of 2.00% on deposits (DFR), 2.15% on main refinancing operations (MRO), and 2.40% on the marginal lending facility (MLF).

  • Bank A has €1bn spare tonight. It will not lend it to Bank B below 2.00%, because the ECB pays 2.00% with no risk.
  • Bank B needs €1bn tonight. It will not pay more than 2.40%, because it can borrow from the ECB at 2.40% (if it has collateral).
  • So the overnight rate between banks ends up between 2.00% and 2.40%. That is the corridor.

If the ECB cuts by 25 bps, the whole corridor moves to 1.75% to 2.15%, and the overnight rate follows the same day.

Since September 2024 the gap between the DFR and the MRO is 0.15%, and the gap between the MRO and the MLF is still 0.25%.

docs.title: Corridor system or floor system
docs.text:
Where the market rate sits inside the corridor depends on how many reserves there are.

Scarce reserves (corridor system) Abundant reserves (floor system) Situation Banks have just about the reserves they need Banks have far more reserves than they need Central bank's job Adjust the amount of reserves every day to aim for the middle of the corridor Set the floor rate, quantity is no longer the issue Where the market rate sits Near the middle, close to the main rate Stuck to the floor Example ECB and Fed before 2008 ECB and Fed after the QE years

After the 2008 crisis and quantitative easing (QE, see below), the system is flooded with reserves. Nobody needs to borrow, everyone has cash to place. So the market rate drops to the floor. That is why €STR (the euro overnight benchmark, published by the ECB) trades a few basis points below the DFR. In March 2024 the ECB confirmed it steers policy through the DFR.

docs.title: On the Fed side
docs.text:
The Fed has also run an "ample reserves" system since 2008. Its tools, with example levels for a 4.25% to 4.50% range.

Tool Role Example ON RRP (overnight reverse repo facility) Floor. The Fed borrows cash from money market funds against Treasuries, including from firms that cannot hold reserves 4.25% (bottom of the range) IORB (interest on reserve balances) The rate paid to banks on their reserves, the main tool 4.40% EFFR (effective fed funds rate) The market rate that results about 4.33% Standing Repo Facility and discount window Ceiling. The Fed lends against collateral 4.50% (top of the range)

The ON RRP exists because money market funds cannot hold reserves at the Fed. Without that floor they would lend their cash below the range.

docs.title: How the rate spreads
docs.text:
policy rate
  -> overnight rates (fed funds, €STR, SOFR, repo)     same day
  -> front end of the curve (T-bills, 2y bonds)        through expectations
  -> swaps, mortgages, corporate loans
  -> borrowing, spending, hiring
  -> inflation                                          12 to 24 months later

docs.title: Step 1, overnight
docs.text: Overnight rates move on the day of the decision, mechanically, through the corridor arbitrage. SOFR (the US repo rate, episode 11) and €STR follow.

docs.title: Step 2, the curve, through expectations
docs.text:
A 2-year rate does not follow today's decision. It follows what the market expects from every decision over the next 2 years. As a first approximation:

2y rate ≈ average of expected overnight rates over 2 years + term premium

The term premium is the small extra that investors ask for locking their money up for longer.

Example. The overnight rate is 4.00%. The market expects an average of 4.00% in year one and 3.00% in year two (cuts are coming).

2y rate ≈ (4.00% + 3.00%) / 2 = 3.50%   (+ a small term premium)

The 2-year is already below overnight even though the central bank has not done anything yet. That is exactly what creates an inverted curve. An inverted curve is the market pricing future rate cuts.

docs.title: Step 3, the real economy
docs.text: Banks fund themselves at rates linked to overnight and the front end of the curve. When their funding cost rises, they lend more expensively to households and companies. A floating-rate mortgage moves quickly (episode 1). A fixed-rate one follows long-term rates more.

docs.title: How the market prices future decisions
docs.text:
On a desk nobody says "I think the Fed will cut". People say "the market is pricing 3 cuts this year". That number comes from OIS swaps (overnight index swaps), swaps whose floating leg is the overnight rate (same logic as episode 10), and from fed funds futures.

Example. Overnight at 4.00%. The market expects a 25 bp cut every quarter starting in 3 months.

months 0-3   : 4.00%
months 3-6   : 3.75%
months 6-9   : 3.50%
months 9-12  : 3.25%
average      : 3.625%

So the 1-year OIS trades around 3.625%. Reading that rate, a trader says "3 cuts priced over the year". If 1-year OIS moves to 3.75% after a strong jobs number, the market has taken out part of a cut.

Important consequence, a decision that is already priced does not move the market. If everyone expects a 25 bp cut and it happens, the curve barely moves. What moves the market is the surprise, or what the central bank says about what comes next (forward guidance).

docs.title: The mandate
docs.text:
Central bank Mandate Fed Dual mandate, maximum employment and stable prices. 2% inflation target (formalised in 2012) ECB Price stability first. Symmetric 2% target over the medium term (2021 strategy review) BoE 2% target set by the government
  • Inflation too high -> hike. Borrowing costs more, saving pays more, so households and companies spend less, demand slows, and prices rise more slowly.
  • Economy too weak, inflation low -> cut. Borrowing gets cheaper, which supports investment and spending.

docs.title: The lag
docs.text: The effect on inflation often takes 12 to 24 months, and the delay is not stable (Milton Friedman talked about long and variable lags). So a central bank decides on forecasts, not on this month's number. If it waited for inflation to be back at 2% before it stopped hiking, it would already have hiked too much.

docs.title: Nominal and real rates
docs.text:
The real rate is the nominal rate minus inflation.

policy rate 4%, inflation 3%  -> real rate = 1%    (fairly restrictive)
policy rate 2%, inflation 5%  -> real rate = −3%   (very loose)

What slows the economy is the real rate. In 2021-2022 policy rates were still close to zero while inflation was above 5%, so policy stayed very loose even after the first hikes.

docs.title: The Taylor rule
docs.text:
A reference economists use to judge whether the rate is "at the right level" (John Taylor, 1993).

rate = r* + inflation + 0.5 × (inflation − 2%) + 0.5 × output gap
  • r* = the neutral real rate, the one that neither slows nor speeds up the economy. You cannot observe it, you estimate it (often around 0.5% to 1%).
  • output gap = the gap in % between what the economy produces and what it could produce without creating inflation.

Example. r* = 1%, inflation = 4%, output gap = 0.

rate = 1% + 4% + 0.5 × (4% − 2%) + 0 = 6%

If the policy rate is at 4%, the rule says it is too low. No central bank applies it mechanically, but markets and journalists use it as a benchmark.

docs.title: When the rate is at zero, QE and QT
docs.text:
A central bank cannot go much below zero. The ECB still had a negative DFR from June 2014 to July 2022 (down to −0.50%). When the policy rate cannot go lower, there is another tool.

  • QE (quantitative easing). The central bank buys large amounts of government bonds with reserves it creates. That pushes bond prices up, so long-term rates down. It also creates the excess reserves that moved systems to floor mode.
  • QT (quantitative tightening). The reverse. The central bank lets its bonds mature without replacing them, or sells them. Reserves shrink.

The policy rate works on the front end of the curve, QE and QT work more on the long end.

docs.title: Real cases
docs.text:
• Volcker, 1979-1981. US inflation goes above 14% in 1980. Paul Volcker, Fed chair, lets the fed funds rate rise to around 20%. Severe recession, but inflation falls below 4% by 1983. It is the historical reference for a central bank breaking inflation.
  • 2008 and 2020. Rates cut to zero and massive QE in both crises.
  • 2022-2023. The Fed goes from 0% to 0.25% (March 2022) to 5.25% to 5.50% (July 2023), including 4 consecutive 0.75% hikes in 2022. The fastest cycle since the 1980s. The ECB hikes in July 2022 for the first time in 11 years. The US 2-year goes from under 1% to over 4% during 2022, and the 2s10s curve stays inverted for about two years.
  • September 2024. The Fed cuts by 0.50%. Four months later the US 10-year rate is about 1% higher. The market raised its growth and inflation expectations and the term premium went up. A policy rate cut does not guarantee lower long-term rates.

docs.title: Classic pitfalls
docs.text:
• "The central bank sets loan rates." No. It sets overnight. The rest is set by the market, which adds its expectations, the term premium and credit risk (episode 5).
  • "A hike always lifts the whole curve." No. If the market thinks the hike will hurt growth, long rates can fall. The curve flattens or inverts.
  • "The decision moves the market." Only the part that was not expected. On the day, you compare the decision and the statement with what was priced.
  • Basis points. 25 bps = 0.25%, not 25%. And a "25 bp hike" on a Fed range moves both ends.
  • Nominal vs real. A 5% rate with 6% inflation is not restrictive.
  • Unsecured vs secured overnight. Fed funds is an unsecured loan between banks. SOFR is repo, so it is secured by Treasuries. They are close but not the same rate.

docs.title: The link with duration
docs.text:
When the market prices more hikes, rates go up and bond prices go down. How much is given by duration.

Example. A 2-year bond has a duration of about 1.9. A hawkish surprise (tougher than expected) lifts the 2-year by 0.50%.

price change ≈ −1.9 × 0.50% = −0.95%

On €10m notional that is a loss of about €95,000. In DV01 terms, about €1,900 per basis point.

docs.title: The S&T interview angle
docs.text:
"How does the Fed actually set rates?" It sets a target range for the fed funds rate and enforces it with administered rates. IORB pays banks on their reserves, ON RRP puts a floor for money market funds, and the Standing Repo Facility acts as a ceiling. Because reserves are abundant, the market rate sits near the bottom of the range.

"The Fed cuts 25 bps, what does the 2-year do?" It depends on what was priced. If the cut was expected, almost nothing. The 2-year reacts to the surprise and to the message about the next meetings.

"Why does the curve invert?" Because the market expects rate cuts, often because it expects a slowdown. Short rates are held by the current policy rate, longer rates include the future cuts.

"How do you know how many cuts are priced?" By reading OIS swaps and fed funds futures, and comparing forward rates with today's overnight rate.

"Your trade if you think the Fed will cut more than the market prices?" Receive fixed on a short-dated swap (a receiver), or buy 2-year bonds. If the cuts come, short rates fall and the position makes money.

"Corridor vs floor system?" Corridor when reserves are scarce and the central bank adjusts the quantity to aim for the middle. Floor when reserves are abundant and the market rate sticks to the deposit rate.

docs.title: Links to previous episodes
docs.text:
• Fixed vs Floating, floating-rate debt follows the policy rate directly.
  • The Yield Curve, the policy rate anchors the left end of the curve.
  • Duration and DV01, what a bond loses when expectations move.
  • Interest Rate Swaps, the fixed rate on a swap is the market's bet on future policy rates.
  • Repo, repo rates and SOFR sit inside the corridor.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text:
• The central bank is the bank of the banks. Only it can create reserves, which lets it control the overnight rate.
  • It does not impose any rate. It sets a floor (what it pays on deposits) and a ceiling (what it charges to lend), and arbitrage does the rest.
  • With abundant reserves, the market rate sticks to the floor. That is the case for the Fed and the ECB today.
  • Overnight moves the same day. The rest of the curve moves on expectations of the next decisions.
  • A decision that is already priced barely moves anything. The surprise is what counts.
  • Hike when inflation is too high, cut when the economy is too weak, with a 12 to 24 month lag, so decisions are made on forecasts.

docs.title: 27. QE and QT
docs.text: Episode 27

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text:
Episode 26 explained how a central bank controls the overnight rate. But in 2008 and again in 2020, central banks took that rate to zero and the economy still needed help. The policy rate only controls day-to-day money, while mortgages, corporate loans and government borrowing are priced off long-term rates (5, 10, 30 years). QE is the tool used to push those long rates down. QT is the reverse.

This episode explains how it works in the balance sheets, why it lowers rates, what it did in practice, and above all the times it went wrong, and why.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
QE (quantitative easing). The central bank buys large amounts of bonds, mostly government bonds (the Fed also bought MBS, bonds backed by mortgages, see episode 8). It pays for them with reserves it creates.

QT (quantitative tightening). The reverse. The central bank shrinks its balance sheet, either by not reinvesting the bonds that mature (passive QT) or by selling them on the market (active QT).

Important point, the central bank does not buy bonds directly from the government. It buys them on the secondary market, from investors (pension funds, insurers, banks). Financing governments directly is forbidden for the ECB by the European treaties.

docs.title: What happens in the balance sheets
docs.text:
The Fed buys $1bn of Treasuries from a pension fund.

Who Assets Liabilities Fed +$1bn Treasuries +$1bn reserves (owed to the fund's bank) The fund's bank +$1bn reserves at the Fed +$1bn deposit (owed to the pension fund) Pension fund −$1bn Treasuries, +$1bn deposit

Three consequences.

  1. The pension fund swapped a bond for cash.
  2. The bank ends up with new reserves, created by the Fed.
  3. The Fed's balance sheet grew by $1bn.

Do that for trillions and the banking system is flooded with reserves. That is exactly why the Fed and the ECB now run a floor system, with the market rate stuck to the deposit rate (episode 26).

QT goes the other way. When a bond held by the Fed matures, the Treasury repays the Fed. The money leaves the Treasury's account, so the Treasury has to borrow again from private investors, who pay with bank deposits. At the end of the chain, reserves disappear.

docs.title: 1. The price effect
docs.text:
A huge buyer shows up, bond prices go up, and when a bond's price goes up its yield goes down.

Example. A 10-year bond has a duration of about 9. If the buying pushes its price up 4%:

yield drop ≈ 4% / 9 ≈ 0.45%

docs.title: 2. Less duration available (the scarcity effect)
docs.text: The central bank takes long bonds out of investors' hands. Those who still need long assets (a life insurer has to cover 30-year liabilities) compete for what is left, so they accept a lower yield. In practice it is the term premium that falls, the extra yield demanded for locking money up for a long time.

docs.title: 3. Portfolio rebalancing
docs.text: The pension fund now holds cash that pays almost nothing. It puts it into corporate bonds or stocks. Credit spreads tighten and stocks go up. That is intended, the central bank wants the whole structure of rates to fall, not just government yields.

docs.title: 4. The signal
docs.text: Buying bonds for years tells the market that policy rates will stay low for a long time. Expected future short rates fall, and so do long rates.

docs.title: Orders of magnitude
docs.text: Fed research on the first QE (Gagnon, Raskin, Remache and Sack, 2011) estimates it lowered the US 10-year yield by roughly 0.3% to 1%, mostly through the term premium. Later programmes are estimated to have had smaller effects, because markets already expected them.

docs.title: Fed
docs.text:
Programme Dates What was bought QE1 Nov 2008 to 2010 MBS and agency debt, then Treasuries from March 2009 (about $1.75tn in total) QE2 Nov 2010 to June 2011 $600bn of Treasuries QE3 Sept 2012 to Oct 2014 No fixed total, $40bn of MBS a month, then an extra $45bn of Treasuries a month Covid QE March 2020 to March 2022 Unlimited at first, then $120bn a month

The Fed's balance sheet went from about $900bn before 2008 to about $4.5tn in 2015, then close to $9tn at the 2022 peak.

docs.title: ECB
docs.text:
• January 2015, launch of the APP (asset purchase programme) with government bond buying, €60bn a month from March 2015.
  • March 2020, PEPP (pandemic emergency purchase programme), with the envelope raised to €1.85tn.
  • APP reinvestments stopped in July 2023, PEPP reinvestments at the end of 2024.

docs.title: Bank of Japan
docs.text: The QE pioneer, from 2001. In 2013, QQE (quantitative and qualitative easing). In 2016 it added yield curve control, targeting the 10-year yield directly around 0% and buying as much as needed to hold it. It ended up owning more than half of Japanese government debt. It left negative rates and yield curve control in March 2024, with its first rate hike in 17 years.

docs.title: QT in practice
docs.text:
• Fed, 2017-2019. First QT, gradual runoff, stopped in 2019 (see the September 2019 repo episode below).
  • Fed, from June 2022. Passive QT with monthly caps raised to $95bn a month ($60bn Treasuries, $35bn MBS). The Treasury cap was cut to $25bn in June 2024, then to $5bn in April 2025, and the Fed ended balance sheet runoff on 1 December 2025.
  • BoE. The only major central bank running active QT, selling gilts on the market from November 2022.

Why slow down and then stop? Because in a floor system you need enough reserves for the rate to stay at the floor. Take out too many and money markets tighten. That is exactly what happened in 2019.

docs.title: 1. The taper tantrum, 2013
docs.text:
What happened. In May 2013, Fed chair Ben Bernanke told Congress the Fed could slow its purchases ("tapering") in the coming meetings. He did not talk about stopping, selling, or hiking. The US 10-year yield went from about 1.6% in early May to close to 3% by September. Emerging market currencies and bonds sold off hard (India, Indonesia, Brazil, Turkey and South Africa, nicknamed the "Fragile Five").

Why. QE had crushed the term premium and pushed investors into riskier assets, including emerging market debt. Just the signal that the main buyer would slow down was enough for the market to put the term premium back in at once and for money to leave emerging markets. The market reacts to expectations, not to the purchases themselves.

The lesson. Exiting QE has to be communicated very slowly and very early. Since then the Fed announces its balance sheet plans months in advance.

docs.title: 2. The repo panic, September 2019
docs.text:
What happened. On 17 September 2019, the US overnight repo rate spiked. SOFR printed 5.25% while the fed funds range was 2.00% to 2.25%, and some trades went through around 10% during the day. The effective fed funds rate broke above its range.

Why. The first QT had taken reserves from about $2.8tn (2014) down to about $1.4tn. That day, two cash drains landed at the same time. Companies paid their quarterly taxes, and purchases of newly issued Treasuries settled. Both moved cash from banks into the Treasury's account at the Fed. Banks that still had reserves did not want to go below their regulatory and internal buffers, so nobody lent. The system no longer had enough reserves to run as a floor system.

The response. The Fed injected cash through repo operations from the next day, then started buying T-bills again (about $60bn a month from October 2019) to rebuild reserves. In 2021 it created a permanent repo facility (the Standing Repo Facility, episode 26).

The lesson. There is a minimum level of reserves, and nobody knows exactly where it is until they hit it. That is why the 2022 QT was slowed and then stopped before getting there.

docs.title: 3. The gilt and LDI crisis, UK, September 2022
docs.text:
What happened. On 23 September 2022, the UK government presented a "mini-budget" with large unfunded tax cuts. Gilts (UK government bonds) sold off violently. The 30-year yield went from about 3.7% to above 5% in a few days. On 28 September the BoE announced it would buy long gilts, up to £5bn a day, at the very moment it was about to start selling them as part of its QT.

Why. Many UK defined-benefit pension funds used LDI strategies (liability-driven investment). To hedge their long-term liabilities, they took exposure to long gilts with leverage, through swaps and repo. When rates jump, those positions lose money and counterparties ask for more collateral (margin calls). To raise that cash, funds sell gilts, which pushes rates up further, which triggers new margin calls. A spiral. The BoE stepped in as buyer of last resort to break it.

The response. Temporary purchases from 28 September to 14 October 2022, about £19bn in total, and the start of QT sales pushed back to 1 November. Leverage rules for LDI funds were tightened afterwards.

The lesson. QT and fiscal policy can collide. And a central bank can end up doing QE and QT at the same time, for two different goals (financial stability on one side, monetary policy on the other).

docs.title: 4. Silicon Valley Bank, March 2023
docs.text:
What happened. SVB, the 16th largest US bank, failed on 10 March 2023 after two days of massive withdrawals.

Why it is linked to QE. During Covid QE, bank deposits exploded (the reserves created by the Fed end up as deposits, see the balance sheets above). SVB's deposits roughly tripled between 2019 and 2021. SVB put a large part of that money into long Treasuries and MBS at very low yields. When the Fed raised rates in 2022, the price of those bonds fell (that is duration). Unrealised losses reached about $15bn at the end of 2022, roughly the size of its equity. When SVB had to sell some of those securities at a loss to pay out deposits, clients panicked and pulled their money.

The lesson. QE creates deposits that banks have to put somewhere. If they go into long bonds without a hedge, the exit from QE and rising rates turn that into a huge rate risk.

docs.title: 5. Central bank losses
docs.text:
What happened. The Fed started posting losses in September 2022. It books them as a "deferred asset" (to be repaid from future profits), which went above $200bn. The BoE lost money on its QE portfolio, and the UK Treasury covers those losses. The ECB reported a loss for 2023, its first since the early 2000s.

Why. During QE the central bank bought bonds paying 1% or 2% and funded them with reserves. When it raises rates to 4% or 5%, it pays that rate on reserves (IORB, episode 26). It earns 1-2% and pays 4-5%, so it loses money. That is negative carry, like a bank that borrows at a higher rate than it lends.

Why it is not a bankruptcy. A central bank cannot go bust in its own currency, since it creates it. The real cost is political and fiscal. It stops sending profits to the government for years, and its losses become a political debate.

docs.title: Classic pitfalls
docs.text:
• "QE is printing banknotes." No. QE creates reserves, which only banks hold. It is not money landing directly in households' pockets. The effect on inflation goes through rates and asset prices.
  • "QE finances the government." Not directly. Purchases happen on the secondary market. But in practice QE makes government borrowing cheaper, hence the debate.
  • "QE caused the 2021-2022 inflation." The 2009-2014 QE did not create inflation. The 2021-2022 inflation came from a mix of shocks (supply chains, energy, large fiscal stimulus, post-Covid demand). The exact role of Covid QE is still debated.
  • "QT means selling bonds." Usually not. The Fed and the ECB run passive QT, they just let bonds mature.
  • The stock matters more than the flow. What weighs on long rates is the total amount of bonds the central bank holds, not this month's pace of buying.

docs.title: The S&T interview angle
docs.text:
"Explain QE." The central bank buys bonds on the market with reserves it creates. That pushes prices up and long yields down, mostly by compressing the term premium, pushes investors into riskier assets, and signals that rates will stay low.

"Difference between cutting the policy rate and doing QE?" The policy rate works on the front end of the curve, QE on the long end. QE is used when the policy rate is already at zero.

"What does QT do to the curve?" It puts duration back into the market, so it pushes the term premium and long rates up. A steepening effect.

"Why did the Fed stop QT?" To avoid falling back into scarce reserves like September 2019, when repo spiked.

"Walk me through the LDI crisis." A sharp jump in long rates after the mini-budget, margin calls on pension funds' leveraged positions, forced gilt sales, a spiral, and the BoE stepping in as buyer of last resort.

"Why do central banks lose money?" They pay the policy rate on the reserves created during QE, while the bonds they bought pay much less.

docs.title: Links to previous episodes
docs.text:
• The Policy Rate, the tool for the front end, and the floor system QE created.
  • The Yield Curve, QE flattens the curve, QT steepens it.
  • Duration and DV01, to size the effect of purchases and SVB's losses.
  • Credit Spread, portfolio rebalancing tightens spreads.
  • Repo, the market that broke in September 2019.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text:
• QE is the central bank buying bonds with reserves it creates. QT is the reverse.
  • It is used to push long rates down when the policy rate is already at zero, mostly by crushing the term premium.
  • It flooded banks with reserves, which is why we have today's floor system.
  • What can go wrong. Just signalling the exit makes rates jump (2013). Too much QT dries up repo (2019). Leveraged positions built on low rates break when rates rise (LDI 2022, SVB 2023). And the central bank loses money when it hikes.

docs.title: 28. FX Forwards
docs.text: Episode 28

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: The last two episodes (the policy rate, QE and QT) explained how each central bank sets the price of money in its own currency. This episode opens the foreign exchange market (FX) through the most direct link with all that. The gap between two countries' interest rates sets the price at which you can exchange those two currencies in the future. Not a forecast, an arbitrage calculation you can redo by hand.

docs.title: Reading an exchange rate
docs.text:
EUR/USD = 1.10 means 1 euro costs 1.10 dollars.

  • The first currency (EUR) is the base currency. You always price 1 unit of the base.
  • The second (USD) is the quote currency, the one the price is written in.
  • If EUR/USD goes to 1.12, you get more dollars for 1 euro, so the euro got stronger and the dollar weaker.
  • If EUR/USD goes to 1.08, the euro got weaker.

docs.title: The pip
docs.text: A pip is the 4th decimal, 0.0001. Going from 1.1000 to 1.1050 is a 50 pip move. Exception, for pairs with the yen (USD/JPY = 150.00) the pip is the 2nd decimal, 0.01, because one yen is worth very little.

docs.title: Bid, ask and spread
docs.text:
A bank always quotes two prices, for example EUR/USD 1.1000 / 1.1002.

  • Bid (1.1000), the price at which the bank buys euros for dollars.
  • Ask (1.1002), the price at which it sells them.
  • The gap (2 pips) is the bank's margin. On the big pairs it is tiny, on thinly traded currencies it can be tens of pips.

docs.title: Quoting conventions
docs.text: You do not choose the order of the currencies freely. The market follows a hierarchy. EUR comes before GBP, which comes before AUD, NZD, USD, CAD, CHF, then JPY. Hence EUR/USD, GBP/USD, USD/JPY, USD/CHF. The dollar is the base against most other currencies, but not against the euro or the pound.

docs.title: Market size
docs.text: FX is the largest financial market in the world. The BIS triennial survey (the BIS is the central banks' bank) measured about $7.5tn traded per day in April 2022, about half of it in FX swaps (see below). The dollar is on one side of roughly 9 trades out of 10.

docs.title: Spot and forward
docs.text:
• Spot. You exchange today, at today's rate. In practice settlement happens 2 business days later (T+2), with a few exceptions like USD/CAD (T+1).
  • Forward. You agree today on a rate, but the exchange happens later, for example in 1 year. Nothing changes hands before that date. The rate is locked.

docs.title: The question
docs.text:
EUR/USD is at 1.10 today. What rate should a bank give you to exchange in 1 year?

You might think it guesses where the euro will be in a year. It does not guess anything. It only uses the spot rate and the interest rate in each currency.

docs.title: The example, two paths
docs.text:
You have €100 and want dollars in 1 year.

  • Interest rate on euros, 2% a year.
  • Interest rate on dollars, 4% a year.
  • Spot, 1.10.

Path 1, exchange now, then save in dollars.

€100 × 1.10 = $110 today
$110 saved at 4% for 1 year -> 110 × 1.04 = $114.40

In a year you have $114.40.

Path 2, save in euros, then exchange in a year.

€100 saved at 2% for 1 year -> 100 × 1.02 = €102
In a year you exchange €102 at the forward rate F -> 102 × F dollars

docs.title: Why both paths must give the same amount
docs.text:
Both paths have zero risk. From day one you know exactly what you will get.

If path 1 gave more dollars than path 2, everyone would do path 1 and the reverse of path 2 at the same time (borrow dollars, exchange into euros, save in euros, sell them back at the forward), and make money with no risk. Banks would lose every time. So the forward rate is set so that both paths give exactly the same result.

102 × F = 114.40
F = 114.40 / 102 = 1.1216

The 1-year forward is 1.1216.

docs.title: The formula
docs.text:
It is the same calculation written in general. It is called covered interest parity (CIP).

Forward = Spot × (1 + quote currency rate × T) / (1 + base currency rate × T)
  • T = time in years (6 months = 0.5, 3 months = 0.25).
  • The quote currency's rate (the 2nd one) goes on top. The base currency's rate (the 1st one) goes at the bottom.

For EUR/USD, the dollar is the quote currency.

1 year   : 1.10 × (1 + 0.04) / (1 + 0.02)             = 1.1216
6 months : 1.10 × (1 + 0.04 × 0.5) / (1 + 0.02 × 0.5) = 1.10 × 1.02 / 1.01 = 1.1109

For more than a year you use compounded rates, (1 + r)^T instead of (1 + r × T). And on a desk you count days exactly, with each currency's convention (actual days / 360 for the dollar and the euro, actual days / 365 for the pound).

docs.title: What it means
docs.text:
In a year you get 1.1216 dollars per euro instead of 1.10. On the forward, the euro is worth a bit more and the dollar a bit less.

The rule, the currency with the higher interest rate is cheaper on the forward. It trades at a forward discount. The other trades at a forward premium.

Why? Dollars pay 2% more than euros. If the forward did not adjust, you would switch your euros into dollars, earn the extra 2%, and lock in your way back into euros with the forward, with no risk at all. The forward takes exactly that 2% back. No free lunch.

docs.title: Forward points
docs.text:
The gap between forward and spot is called the forward points.

1.1216 − 1.10 = 0.0216 = 216 pips

On a screen, banks do not quote the full forward. They quote the spot and the points (+216). The full forward (1.1216) is called the outright.

Quick approximation, the points are roughly spot × rate gap × T. Here 1.10 × 2% × 1 = 0.022, so about 220 pips.

docs.title: Second example, USD/JPY
docs.text:
Spot USD/JPY = 150. Dollar rate 4%, yen rate 0.5%. Here the dollar is the base currency, so its rate goes at the bottom.

1-year forward = 150 × (1 + 0.005) / (1 + 0.04) = 150 × 1.005 / 1.04 = 144.95

The forward is lower than spot. That makes sense, the base currency (the dollar) has the higher rate, so it is the one trading at a discount. Forward points, 144.95 − 150 = −5.05 yen, so −505 pips (a yen pip is 0.01).

Same rule, the currency that pays more is cheaper in the future. Only the way it shows up in the number changes, depending on whether it is the base or the quote.

docs.title: The forward is not a forecast
docs.text:
This is the most important and most misunderstood point. The 1.1216 forward does not say the market thinks the euro will rise. It is just the result of the arbitrage. If the rates were the other way around (euro at 4%, dollar at 2%), the forward would be below spot, whatever the market thinks of the euro.

The "forecast" version of the formula exists, it is uncovered interest parity (UIP). It would say the higher-yielding currency will weaken by the rate gap. In practice it does not work. Studies show high-yielding currencies tend not to weaken that much, and sometimes even rise (the "forward premium puzzle", Fama, 1984). That is what makes the carry trade possible, borrowing in the low-rate currency and investing in the high-rate one, while keeping the currency risk. It often earns a little, and sometimes loses a lot at once.

An example of that, August 2024. For years, investors borrowed in yen (rates near zero) to invest in dollars and elsewhere. At the end of July 2024 the Bank of Japan raised rates and the yen rallied. USD/JPY went from about 162 in early July to about 142 on 5 August. Those who had borrowed in yen had to pay back more, they all cut their positions at the same time, which pushed the yen up further. On 5 August 2024 the Nikkei lost about 12% in one session.

Key difference. The forward (CIP) is covered, so there is no currency risk, and arbitrage makes it hold. The carry trade (UIP) is not covered, so you take the currency risk, and nothing forces the formula to hold.

docs.title: A company hedging its FX risk
docs.text:
A French company will receive $10m in 1 year. Its costs are in euros. It does not know what the dollar will be worth in a year, so it sells its dollars forward today, at 1.1216.

$10,000,000 / 1.1216 = €8,915,835
EUR/USD in 1 year Unhedged With the forward 1.00 €10,000,000 €8,915,835 1.1216 €8,915,835 €8,915,835 1.25 €8,000,000 €8,915,835

With the forward it knows its number to the cent. It gives up the good case (1.00) to protect itself from the bad case (1.25). It is the same trade-off as an interest rate swap, you swap uncertainty for a fixed number.

docs.title: The FX swap, a loan in disguise
docs.text:
An FX swap combines two operations in one trade. An exchange at spot today, and the reverse exchange at the forward later.

Example. A European bank needs dollars for 3 months. It gives €100m and receives $110m today at the 1.10 spot. In 3 months it gives the dollars back and gets its €100m back, at the forward rate fixed today.

In practice it is a dollar loan secured by euros. Exactly like a repo, where you borrow cash against securities as collateral, except that here the collateral is another currency. The cost of the loan is hidden in the forward points.

It is the most traded FX product in the world. Non-US banks, Japanese insurers buying US bonds, European asset managers, they all use it to fund or hedge themselves in dollars.

docs.title: NDFs
docs.text: Some currencies cannot be exchanged freely abroad (capital controls). For those, people use NDFs (non-deliverable forwards). Nobody delivers the currency. At maturity you compare the forward rate with the actual rate on the day and only settle the difference, in dollars. It is common for currencies like the Brazilian real, the Indian rupee or the Korean won.

docs.title: Where the formula breaks a bit, the cross-currency basis
docs.text:
Before 2008 the formula held almost perfectly. Since then there has been a persistent gap.
