Example. With the rates from the example, the theoretical 3-month forward is:

1.10 × (1 + 0.04 × 0.25) / (1 + 0.02 × 0.25) = 1.10 × 1.01 / 1.005 = 1.1055

Say the market actually quotes 1.1062. What dollar rate does that imply?

1 + implied dollar rate × 0.25 = 1.1062 × 1.005 / 1.10 = 1.0107
implied dollar rate ≈ 4.27%

Borrowing dollars through the FX swap costs 4.27%, while the "normal" dollar rate is 4.00%. That gap of about 27 basis points is the cross-currency basis. By convention it is written as negative (here about −27 bps) when borrowing dollars through FX costs more than the formula says.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
• Balance sheet cost. To arbitrage the gap, a bank has to borrow and lend, so grow its balance sheet. Since 2008, capital rules (the leverage ratio in particular) make that expensive. The arbitrage still exists but it is no longer free, so it does not fully close the gap.
  • Demand for dollars. Many non-US players need dollars (banks, Japanese insurers hedging their US bonds, companies with dollar debt). They are willing to pay a bit more.
  • Quarter-ends and year-ends. Banks shrink their balance sheets before reporting dates. The basis often widens around those dates.

docs.title: In a crisis
docs.text: The basis blows out when everyone wants dollars at the same time. In 2008, and again in March 2020. In March 2020 the Fed expanded its swap lines, FX swaps between the Fed and other central banks (ECB, BoJ, BoE, SNB...). It lends them dollars against their currency, and they lend the dollars on to their banks. The basis narrowed in the following weeks. The Fed acts as the dollar lender of last resort for the whole world.

docs.title: Classic pitfalls
docs.text:
• "The forward is what the market expects." No. It is the result of the spot + rates arbitrage. See UIP and CIP above.
  • Putting the rates on the wrong side. The quote currency's rate (the 2nd) on top, the base currency's rate (the 1st) at the bottom. Quick check, the currency with the higher rate must be cheaper on the forward.
  • Mixing up points and outright. "+216" are points, added to spot. The outright is 1.1216.
  • Forgetting the yen pip. On USD/JPY, 1 pip = 0.01, not 0.0001.
  • Simple vs compound interest. Under a year, (1 + r × T). Over a year, (1 + r)^T. And day count conventions differ by currency.
  • Thinking a hedge makes money. It removes uncertainty, it does not create profit. If the dollar rises, the hedged company "loses" compared with the unhedged one.

docs.title: The S&T interview angle
docs.text:
"EUR/USD is at 1.10, euro rate 2%, dollar rate 4%. 1-year forward?" 1.10 × 1.04 / 1.02 = 1.1216. The dollar has the higher rate, so it is cheaper on the forward, so the EUR/USD forward is above spot.

"Why does the higher-rate currency trade at a forward discount?" Otherwise you could borrow in the low-rate currency, invest in the high-rate one, and hedge the way back with the forward for a risk-free profit. The forward cancels out the rate gap.

"Is the forward a forecast?" No, it is an arbitrage price. The forecast would be UIP, which does not hold in the data, and that is why the carry trade exists.

"What is an FX swap and what is it for?" A spot and an opposite forward in the same trade. Economically, a secured loan in another currency. It is used to fund in dollars or to hedge a foreign-currency portfolio.

"What is the cross-currency basis?" The gap between the dollar borrowing cost implied by FX swaps and the direct dollar rate. It exists because arbitrage costs balance sheet since 2008 and because demand for dollars outside the US is strong. It widens in crises and at quarter-ends.

"How did the Fed calm the dollar market in March 2020?" By expanding its swap lines with other central banks, which lent the dollars on to their banks.

docs.title: Links to previous episodes
docs.text:
• The Policy Rate, policy rates set the rates that go into the formula.
  • QE and QT, low rates and then the fast 2022 hikes that moved rate gaps and forwards.
  • Interest Rate Swaps, the same logic of swapping uncertainty for a fixed number.
  • Repo, an FX swap is a secured loan, like a repo with a currency as collateral.
  • Put-Call Parity, the same arbitrage reasoning, two risk-free paths must cost the same.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text:
• EUR/USD = 1.10 means 1 euro costs 1.10 dollars. Base first, quote second.
  • The forward is not a forecast. It is set so that exchanging now and saving, or saving and exchanging later, give the same result.
  • Forward = Spot × (1 + quote rate × T) / (1 + base rate × T).
  • The currency with the higher interest rate is cheaper on the forward. The forward cancels out the rate gap.
  • Companies use it to lock in their exchange rate, banks use FX swaps to borrow dollars.
  • Since 2008, borrowing dollars through FX costs a bit more than the formula says (the cross-currency basis), and the gap blows out in a crisis.

docs.title: 29. The Carry Trade
docs.text: Episode 29

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: Episode 28 showed that the forward is covered. You lock the exchange rate, so you earn nothing more than the risk-free rate. The carry trade is exactly the same setup without the hedge. You keep the interest rate gap, and you take the currency risk. It is one of the most widely used strategies in the market, and it has a very particular shape of risk, small steady gains and big sudden losses.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
You borrow in a low-rate currency (the funding currency), exchange the money into a high-rate currency, invest it, and do not hedge the exchange rate. You collect the rate gap, the carry, as long as the exchange rate does not move against you.

The classic version for years, borrow in yen (rate near 0%) and invest in dollars (4% to 5%). The yen even has a name in this role, the funding currency. People talked about "Mrs Watanabe", the Japanese retail savers who put their money abroad.

docs.title: The worked example
docs.text:
USD/JPY = 150 (1 dollar costs 150 yen). Yen rate 0.5%, dollar rate 4%.

Today.

You borrow ¥15,000,000 at 0.5%
You exchange: 15,000,000 / 150 = $100,000
You invest $100,000 at 4%

In 1 year.

You have:  $100,000 × 1.04     = $104,000
You owe:   ¥15,000,000 × 1.005 = ¥15,075,000

You hold dollars and you owe yen. Everything depends on the exchange rate in a year.

USD/JPY in 1 year $104,000 are worth You repay Result in yen In dollars On $100,000 160 (dollar up) ¥16,640,000 ¥15,075,000 +¥1,565,000 +$9,781 +9.8% 150 (unchanged) ¥15,600,000 ¥15,075,000 +¥525,000 +$3,500 +3.5% 144.95 ¥15,075,000 ¥15,075,000 0 0 0% 140 (yen up) ¥14,560,000 ¥15,075,000 −¥515,000 −$3,679 −3.7% 130 (yen way up) ¥13,520,000 ¥15,075,000 −¥1,555,000 −$11,962 −12.0%

A 6.7% move in the yen (150 to 140) wipes out a whole year of interest, and more.

docs.title: The break-even is the forward
docs.text:
At what rate do you earn nothing?

104,000 × X = 15,075,000
X = 15,075,000 / 104,000 = 144.95

That is exactly the forward rate from the previous episode (150 × 1.005 / 1.04 = 144.95).

So the carry trade is a bet that the exchange rate in a year will be better than the forward. Not better than spot, better than the forward.

docs.title: Same trade, forward version
docs.text:
You can run the same trade without borrowing or investing anything. You buy USD/JPY forward at 144.95. In a year, if spot is at 150, you buy at 144.95 and sell at 150:

profit = 150 − 144.95 = ¥5.05 per dollar  ->  5.05 / 144.95 ≈ 3.5%

Same result as the borrow and invest setup (3.5%). That is why on a desk people say "long USD/JPY forward" to mean "running carry". The forward points (−505 pips, episode 28) are the price of being long the high-rate currency, and the trade wins if spot ends above the forward.

docs.title: Why it works (most of the time)
docs.text:
Episode 28 said that uncovered interest parity (UIP) predicts the high-rate currency should weaken by exactly the rate gap. If that were true, the carry trade would earn zero on average.

In practice it is false. Studies (starting with Fama, 1984) show high-rate currencies weaken less than the rate gap, sometimes not at all. That is the "forward premium puzzle". So the carry trade has made money on average over decades.

docs.title: Why the market lets that exist
docs.text:
The most common answer is that carry is the payment for taking a risk, like the insurance you sell. You collect a small premium every year, and in exchange you accept losing a lot when the market panics. Carry behaves like selling an option, whose payoff we saw in episode 13 (small premium, big possible loss).

Other explanations put forward. Central banks smoothing exchange rates. Investors reacting too slowly to rate gaps. Corporate hedging flows. Nobody has a definitive answer.

docs.title: How it loses, the sudden losses
docs.text: The gains are small and steady (a few % a year). The losses are big and abrupt. Traders say carry goes up the stairs and comes down the elevator. Carry returns have "negative skew", lots of small gains and rare very large losses.

docs.title: Leverage
docs.text:
Almost nobody runs carry without leverage, because 3.5% a year is small. With leverage:

Leverage Gain if nothing moves (3.5%) Loss if USD/JPY goes to 140 (−3.7%) 1x +3.5% −3.7% 5x +17.5% −18.4% 10x +35% −36.8% 20x +70% −73.6%

At 20x leverage, a 6.7% move in the yen destroys three quarters of the capital. And FX brokers force-liquidate well before that.

docs.title: The unwind spiral
docs.text:
Everyone runs the same trade, borrowing yen and selling it. When something scares the market:

  1. Investors close their positions, so they buy back yen to repay their loans.
  2. Buying yen pushes it up.
  3. A stronger yen makes the other carry traders lose money, so they close too (margin calls, stop-losses).
  4. The yen goes up even more.

It is the same mechanism as the UK pension fund spiral in episode 27 (forced selling moves the price, which forces more selling). It is also the same as the gamma squeeze in episode 20, where some people's hedging feeds the move that forces others.

docs.title: 1. October 1998, after LTCM
docs.text:
In the summer of 1998 Russia defaulted on its debt and the fund LTCM collapsed (episode 25). Hedge funds, which had borrowed yen to fund positions everywhere, unwound all at once. On 7 and 8 October 1998, USD/JPY went from about 135 to about 112 in two days, a yen roughly 15% stronger.

Why. Carry positions were huge and concentrated in the same funding currency. When funds needed cash elsewhere, they all bought back yen at the same time.

docs.title: 2. 2008, AUD/JPY
docs.text:
Australia had rates around 7%, Japan around 0.5%. AUD/JPY was the most popular carry pair. It was worth about 107 in July 2008 and about 55 in October 2008. Almost half its value in three months.

Why. The Lehman crisis sent everyone into safe currencies (yen, dollar) and out of high-rate currencies. Over those three months, the carry earned (about 6.5% a year, so about 1.6% over the period) counted for nothing against a 45% fall.

docs.title: 3. January 2015, the Swiss franc
docs.text:
Since 2011 the Swiss central bank (SNB) had held a floor at 1.20 francs per euro. Swiss rates were very low. Many households in Poland, Hungary and other Eastern European countries had borrowed in Swiss francs for their mortgage, because the rate was lower than a loan in local currency. Without knowing it, they were in a carry trade, borrowed in francs, earning in zloty or forint.

On 15 January 2015 the SNB dropped the floor without warning. The franc rose up to about 30% against the euro within minutes, and ended the day roughly 15% to 20% higher.

Consequences. These households' debt rose by the same amount overnight, while their salaries stayed in local currency. FX brokers went bust the same day because clients' losses were bigger than their deposits (for example Alpari UK, and FXCM had to be rescued). The common thread, a position that earns a small carry for years, with a central bank hiding a jump risk.

docs.title: 4. August 2024, the yen
docs.text:
For years, investors around the world had borrowed in yen. At the end of July 2024 the Bank of Japan raised rates and hinted at more hikes. At the same time the Fed signalled cuts, so the rate gap was narrowing from both sides. USD/JPY went from about 162 in early July to about 142 on 5 August, a yen roughly 14% stronger. The Nikkei lost about 12% on 5 August, its worst session since 1987, then almost fully rebounded over the following days.

Why. The rate gap that justified the trade was shrinking (less carry), and the yen was rising (currency loss). Both effects worked in the same direction, so positions closed at the same time.

docs.title: How to judge whether carry is attractive
The carry to volatility ratio
docs.text:
Earning 3.5% does not mean the same thing if the pair moves 5% a year or 15% a year.

carry / vol ratio = rate gap / volatility of the exchange rate

Example. Rate gap 3.5%. - If USD/JPY implied volatility is 7%, ratio = 3.5 / 7 = 0.5. - If it is 14%, ratio = 3.5 / 14 = 0.25.

With the same rate gap, the trade is half as attractive when volatility doubles. Traders look for a high ratio, and a falling ratio (rising volatility) is a warning sign.

docs.title: What options say
docs.text: In episode 21 we saw that put and call prices are not symmetric when the market fears one direction. For a carry pair, the market pays more to protect against a fall in the high-rate currency (so against the unwind). You read it in the risk reversal, the difference in implied volatility between a put and a call of the same delta. When the risk reversal becomes very lopsided, the market is pricing unwind risk.

docs.title: Hedging with options
docs.text: You can buy a put on the high-rate currency (here a USD/JPY put, which gains if the dollar falls against the yen) to cap the loss. It costs premium, which eats part of the carry. It is episode 13 applied to FX. The trade becomes carry with a loss floor, and its profitability depends on the ratio between the carry received and the premium paid.

docs.title: Carry is not only FX
docs.text:
The word "carry" generally means what you earn if nothing moves.

Market What the trade does The carry The risk FX Long the high-rate currency, short the low-rate one The rate gap The unwind, a currency jump Bonds Buy a long bond funded in short repo The coupon minus the repo cost Rates rise (duration) Yield curve Pay or receive in a swap, sit on the slope of the curve Roll-down (the bond gets closer to maturity and slides down the curve) The curve moves Credit Sell protection on a CDS The premium received Default Options Sell an option, see theta The premium that decays The big move

Same structure every time. A small steady income, against a big rare loss.

docs.title: Classic pitfalls
docs.text:
• Thinking carry is a free gain. As long as you do not hedge, it is not riskless at all. The gain is payment for currency risk.
  • Comparing to spot instead of the forward. The break-even is the forward (144.95), not spot (150). That small gap is the difference between winning and losing.
  • Forgetting leverage. The numbers on unlevered carry are small. Leverage is what makes the trade attractive, and what makes it dangerous.
  • Jump risk on a managed exchange rate. When a central bank defends a floor or a cap (Swiss franc in 2015), the risk is hidden until the day it jumps all at once.
  • Trusting recent volatility. Volatility is low just before unwinds, because carry is working well. A very high carry to vol ratio can be a sign of complacency rather than a good deal.
  • Costs. Bid-ask, funding the leverage, daily rollover. On 3.5% of carry, they matter.

docs.title: The S&T interview angle
docs.text:
"What is a carry trade?" Borrowing in a low-rate currency, investing in a high-rate currency, without hedging the exchange rate. You earn the rate gap as long as the high-rate currency does not weaken by more than that gap.

"Where is the break-even?" At the forward rate. If the final spot is better than the forward, the trade wins, otherwise it loses.

"Why does it work, when uncovered parity says the opposite?" High-rate currencies weaken on average by less than the rate gap (forward premium puzzle). Carry is also payment for taking unwind risk.

"What is the risk profile?" Small steady gains, big abrupt losses. Negative skew, like selling an option.

"Why do losses all arrive at the same time?" Everyone runs the same trade, so when a shock hits, everyone closes at once, which moves the price against everyone else. A spiral of forced selling.

"Give examples." 1998 after LTCM, 2008 AUD/JPY, 2015 Swiss franc, August 2024 yen.

"How do you hedge it?" With a put on the high-rate currency. It caps the loss but eats part of the carry.

"What is the difference between a carry trade and a forward?" A forward is covered, so it earns nothing more than rates. Carry is not covered, so it can win or lose. Carry is a bet that the final spot will be better than the forward.

docs.title: Links to previous episodes
docs.text:
• FX Forwards, the carry break-even is the forward.
  • QE and QT, the same forced-selling spiral, and rate gaps between countries come from central banks.
  • The Policy Rate, rate decisions create and destroy the gaps.
  • Options, carry looks like selling an option, and an option can hedge it.
  • Volatility Skew, the risk reversal reads the fear of an unwind.
  • Theta, selling options is carry too.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text:
• A carry trade is borrowing in a low-rate currency and investing in a high-rate currency, without hedging the exchange rate.
  • The break-even is the forward rate. The trade wins if the final exchange rate is better than the forward.
  • It wins on average because high-rate currencies weaken less than the rate gap, but that is payment for a risk.
  • The profile is small steady gains, big sudden losses. Leverage amplifies both.
  • Losses arrive together because everyone runs the same trade and exits at the same time (1998, 2008, 2015, 2024).
  • Carry is not only FX. It is also bonds funded in repo, selling CDS and selling options.

docs.title: 30. Pricing Rate Cuts
docs.text: Episode 30

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: Episode 26 said "the market is pricing 3 cuts this year" without showing where that number comes from. It is the most used number on a rates desk. Nobody asks the market what it expects from the central bank. You read it in a price, the price of an OIS. This episode gives the formulas to read that price, two ways to turn it into a probability of a cut, the maths for how much you make or lose when the pricing moves, and three real cases where what the market had priced turned out to be wrong.

docs.title: What an OIS is
docs.text:
OIS = overnight index swap. It is an interest rate swap whose floating leg is the overnight rate (SOFR in the US, €STR in the euro area), compounded day after day over the period.

  • One side pays a fixed rate for the whole period.
  • The other side pays the compounded overnight rate.
  • At the end, only the difference is exchanged.

The fixed rate is chosen so the swap costs nothing on day one. So the fixed rate is the market's best estimate of the average overnight rate over the period. Same reasoning as the fixed rate on a plain swap.

docs.title: Formula 1, the OIS is an average
docs.text:
OIS ≈ average of expected overnight rates over the period
    ≈ (r1 × t1 + r2 × t2 + ... ) / T
  • r1, r2... = the expected overnight rate during each piece of the period.
  • t1, t2... = the length of each piece, in years.
  • T = the total length.

Example. Overnight today, 4.00%. 1-year OIS, 3.625%. The market expects an average of 3.625% over the year, so cuts are coming. How many? Suppose a 25 bps (0.25%) cut every 3 months, the first in 3 months.

months 0-3    4.00%
months 3-6    3.75%
months 6-9    3.50%
months 9-12   3.25%
average       (4.00 + 3.75 + 3.50 + 3.25) / 4 = 3.625%

That matches the OIS. We read "3 cuts priced over the year" by rebuilding the path that gives 3.625%.

This is a simplification. A real OIS compounds the overnight rate day after day, which gives a slightly higher rate than a simple average (here about 3.67% with quarterly compounding). The gap is a few bps, so the method is fine for reading the number of cuts, but a desk uses exact compounding to price.

docs.title: Formula 2, a cut counts according to the time left
docs.text:
A cut decided early weighs more in the average than a cut decided late.

effect on the average = size of the cut × (time left after the decision / T)

With the 3 cuts of 25 bps at 3, 6 and 9 months:

Cut Time left Weight Effect on the 1-year OIS Month 3 9 months 9/12 25 × 0.75 = 18.75 bps Month 6 6 months 6/12 25 × 0.50 = 12.5 bps Month 9 3 months 3/12 25 × 0.25 = 6.25 bps Total 37.5 bps

4.00% − 0.375% = 3.625%. We recover the OIS.

Practical consequence. A 25 bps cut in 3 months only moves the 1-year OIS by 18.75 bps, not 25. To get "how many cuts" from an OIS, you have to account for their dates. A shorter OIS, covering only the next few meetings, gives a cleaner signal.

docs.title: Formula 3, the forward rate between two OIS
docs.text:
You want the expected average for a specific period. You compare two OIS of different lengths.

forward = (R2 × T2 − R1 × T1) / (T2 − T1)

Example. 6-month OIS = 3.875%, 1-year OIS = 3.625%.

6m forward starting in 6m = (3.625 × 1 − 3.875 × 0.5) / (1 − 0.5)
                          = (3.625 − 1.9375) / 0.5
                          = 3.375%

The market expects an average of 3.875% in the first 6 months, then 3.375% in the next 6. It is the same idea as the forward on the yield curve and the FX forward in episode 28, you get the future by comparing two horizons.

docs.title: Formula 4, from OIS to the probability of a cut
docs.text:
The central bank moves in 25 bps steps. The market, on the other hand, prices an average across possible scenarios.

probability of a 25 bps cut ≈ expected cut at the meeting / 25 bps

Example. Current rate 4.00%. The expected rate after the next meeting, read from the OIS, is 3.875%.

expected cut = 4.00 − 3.875 = 12.5 bps
probability  = 12.5 / 25 = 50%

The market prices a 50% chance of a 25 bps cut. If the expected cut is 18.75 bps, it is 75%.

When the market is torn between 25 and 50 bps, the expected cut sits in between. For example, 37.5 bps expected means 50% of 25 bps and 50% of 50 bps.

docs.title: Formula 5, the fed funds future
docs.text:
Same information, futures version. The fed funds futures contract quotes a price.

future price = 100 − expected average rate over the month

Example. Price 96.25, meaning an expected average rate of 100 − 96.25 = 3.75%. A rising price means a falling expected rate, so more cuts priced. The CME FedWatch tool that everyone quotes turns these prices into probabilities with formula 4.

docs.title: Formula 6, how much you make or lose
docs.text:
If you think the central bank will cut more than the market prices, you receive the fixed rate on an OIS. You win if the market's fixed rate falls.

P&L ≈ notional × DV01 per bp × change in OIS (in bps)
DV01 of a 1-year OIS ≈ notional × 0.0001 × 0.96   (duration close to 1 year, discounted)

Example. Notional $100m, 1-year OIS at 3.625%. DV01 ≈ 100,000,000 × 0.0001 × 0.96 ≈ $9,600 per bp. See DV01.

What the market does Change in OIS Receiver's P&L One more 25 bps cut priced at 3 months −18.75 bps +$180,000 One fewer 25 bps cut priced at 3 months +18.75 bps −$180,000 Nothing moves 0 0

(18.75 × 9,600 ≈ 180,000.)

A longer OIS has a bigger DV01. A 2-year OIS has a DV01 about 1.9 times that of a 1-year OIS, same logic as duration.

docs.title: Why the surprise is what counts
docs.text:
market reaction ≈ what happened − what was priced
Priced Decision Surprise Reaction 100% of a 25 cut 25 cut 0 Almost none 50% of a 25 cut 25 cut 12.5 bps more cut Short rates fall 100% of a 25 cut No cut −25 bps Short rates jump 100% of a 25 cut 50 cut +25 bps Short rates fall hard

And not only the decision of the day. Forward guidance (what the chair says about what comes next) moves the rest of the path, so the OIS on the following meetings.

docs.title: 1. March 2023, SVB: the market flips its pricing in 3 days
docs.text:
In early March 2023 the market was pricing more Fed hikes, with a terminal rate close to 5.5%. On 10 March Silicon Valley Bank failed (episode 27). Within days the market removed the hikes and priced cuts before the end of the year. The US 2-year yield, the most sensitive to Fed expectations, fell about 90 bps in three days (between 87 and 97 bps depending on the source and the time of measurement), its biggest three-day fall since the 1987 crash.

The number. A 2-year bond has a duration of about 1.9. A 0.90% fall in yield gives about +1.7% in price, so about €170,000 gained on €10m of notional. A trader who was receiving rates before the weekend made a huge gain, a payer took the loss.

The lesson. Pricing can flip within days when the nature of the risk changes. It was no longer about inflation but about financial stability.

docs.title: 2. 2024, pricing versus reality
docs.text:
December 2023, the Fed publishes its projections, the median member sees 3 cuts of 25 bps in 2024 (75 bps). The market goes further and prices as many as 6 or 7 cuts for the year in early 2024 (about 150 to 175 bps, depending on the date and the measure). Then inflation stays stronger than expected, and the market removes cuts over the following months.

What happened. The Fed cut by 100 bps in 2024 (50 bps in September, then 25 in November and 25 in December). Fewer than the market in early 2024, more than the 75 bps of the December median.

The number. An OIS receiver who entered when 175 bps were priced and exited when only 100 bps were left priced (for example) lost money on the pricing, even though the Fed did cut. To win you had to be right on the number of cuts, not only on the direction.

The lesson. Being right on direction is not enough. You have to be right relative to what is already priced.

docs.title: 3. September 2024, 25 or 50 bps
docs.text:
Ahead of the 18 September 2024 meeting, the market was torn between a 25 and a 50 bps cut. According to CME FedWatch estimates reported in the press, the probability of a 50 bps cut was about 14% the day before a Wall Street Journal article and a comment from Bill Dudley, then about 44% right after (other measures gave a bit more). In early August, after the yen shock (episode 29), it had reached about 70%.

The Fed cut by 50 bps.

The number. With formula 4, a 44% probability of 50 bps gives an expected cut of 25 × 0.56 + 50 × 0.44 = 14 + 22 = 36 bps. So the 50 bps cut was a surprise of +14 bps, small compared with most surprises. It was already largely priced.

The lesson. A big decision is not a big surprise. When pricing has converged before the meeting, the market barely moves, and what matters becomes what the chair says about the path.

docs.title: Classic pitfalls
docs.text:
• "The market prices 3 cuts" without saying over what period. With formula 2, 3 cuts over 12 months and 3 cuts by year-end do not give the same 1-year OIS.
  • Taking the OIS for an exact forecast. It contains a small risk premium and it is the result of a price, not a survey. Useful for reading expectations, not for predicting.
  • Forgetting the meeting dates. A cut in September weighs less on the 1-year OIS than a cut in March.
  • Confusing direction and pricing. Being right that the Fed cuts earns nothing if it is already priced.
  • Turning a probability into a certainty. "44%" means 56% of the market saw something else. It happens.
  • Mixing OIS and classic swap rates. A swap on Libor or Euribor also contains bank credit risk. OIS has (almost) no credit risk, which is why it became the reference for reading expectations.

docs.title: The S&T interview angle
docs.text:
"How do you know how many cuts are priced?" You read the OIS for each meeting and look at the expected cut versus the current rate. Expected cut divided by 25 bps gives the probability of a 25 bps cut.

"The 1-year OIS is at 3.625% and overnight is at 4.00%. What does it mean?" The market expects an average of 3.625% over the year, so 37.5 bps below overnight on average. With 25 bps cuts, that matches 3 cuts spread at 3, 6 and 9 months.

"Your trade if you think the Fed will cut more than the market prices?" Receive fixed on an OIS or buy fed funds futures. I win if the pricing falls, and the size of the gain depends on the DV01.

"Why doesn't a 25 bps cut move the 1-year OIS by 25 bps?" Because the OIS is an average over the period. The effect is weighted by the time left after the cut.

"What if the Fed cuts as expected?" Nothing moves, because it was already priced. The market reacts to the surprise and to forward guidance.

"Why OIS and not Libor?" Because OIS contains almost no bank credit risk, so it reflects monetary policy expectations more cleanly.

docs.text:

  • QE and QT, SVB and the failure that flipped the pricing.
  • Interest Rate Swaps, an OIS is a swap, same mechanics.
  • The Yield Curve, the forward between two OIS follows the same logic as the curve forward.
  • DV01, to size the gain or loss when the pricing moves.
  • FX Forwards, same forward formula between two horizons.
  • The Carry Trade, the August 2024 yen shock flipped Fed pricing.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text:
• An OIS is a swap whose floating leg is the overnight rate. Its fixed rate is the expected average overnight rate over the period.
  • A cut counts according to the time left: effect = size × (time left / total length).
  • Probability of a 25 bps cut ≈ expected cut at the meeting / 25 bps.
  • The forward between two OIS: (R2 × T2 − R1 × T1) / (T2 − T1).
  • An OIS receiver's gain ≈ notional × DV01 × change in bps.
  • The market reacts to the surprise, not to the decision. Being right on direction earns nothing if it is already priced.

docs.title: 31. Inflation Breakevens
docs.text: Episode 31

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: Episodes 26, 27 and 30 covered the "rates" half of a central bank's job. The other half is inflation, and it is the reason central banks hike or cut. This episode shows how to read what the market expects for inflation straight from bond prices. It is a basic tool on a rates desk, it fits in one formula, and it has very clear real cases.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: A normal bond pays a fixed amount, so inflation erodes its real value. A 10-year bond paying 4.20% a year is worth less in purchasing power if prices rise 5% a year. So investors wanted a bond that protects them. It exists.

docs.title: Inflation-linked bonds
docs.text:
In the US they are TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities). In the UK, index-linked gilts ("linkers"). In France, the OATi and OAT€i. The principle is the same.

  • The principal (the amount repaid at the end) is adjusted with the consumer price index (CPI, the basket of prices a country tracks).
  • The coupon is a fixed percentage of that adjusted principal.
  • At maturity you get the adjusted principal back, and in the US never less than the original par (the deflation floor).

Example. $1,000 par, 2% coupon, and prices have risen 3% since issue.

index ratio          = 1.03
adjusted principal   = 1,000 × 1.03 = $1,030
coupon               = 2% × 1,030 = $20.60   (instead of $20.00)

A TIPS yield is called the real yield. It is what you earn above inflation.

docs.title: The breakeven formula
docs.text:
A nominal 10-year pays 4.20%. A 10-year TIPS pays a real yield of 1.90% plus inflation. Which is better depends on the inflation that comes. The inflation level where both give exactly the same result is called the breakeven.

Approximation.

breakeven = nominal yield − real yield
          = 4.20% − 1.90% = 2.30%

Exact version, the Fisher equation.

(1 + nominal) = (1 + real) × (1 + inflation)
inflation     = 1.042 / 1.019 − 1 = 2.26%

docs.title: Check with money
docs.text:
You invest $1 for 10 years in one or the other.

Nominal :  1.042^10                          = 1.509
TIPS    :  (1.019 × (1 + inflation))^10
   inflation 1.00% a year  ->  1.334         nominal wins
   inflation 2.26% a year  ->  1.509         tie
   inflation 3.00% a year  ->  1.622         TIPS wins

Reading.

  • If average inflation over 10 years is above 2.26%, the TIPS wins.
  • If it is below, the nominal wins.

So the breakeven is the market's price of inflation. Someone who thinks inflation will be higher than the breakeven buys the TIPS. Someone who thinks it will be lower buys the nominal.

docs.title: What the breakeven really contains
docs.text:
breakeven = expected inflation + inflation risk premium − liquidity premium
  • Inflation risk premium. The extra yield nominal bond holders want, because surprise inflation hurts them.
  • Liquidity premium. TIPS are harder to trade, so their yield is a bit higher, which lowers the breakeven.

So the breakeven is not a pure forecast. Same lesson as the OIS and the forward, a price that mostly reflects expectations, plus some noise. In a liquidity crisis the noise dominates (March 2020 below).

docs.title: The inflation forward: the 5y5y
docs.text:
You compare two breakevens of different lengths, like the forward between two OIS or the FX forward in episode 28.

(1 + BE10)^10 = (1 + BE5)^5 × (1 + f)^5
f = [ (1 + BE10)^10 / (1 + BE5)^5 ]^(1/5) − 1

Example. 5-year BE = 2.50%, 10-year BE = 2.30%.

f = [ 1.023^10 / 1.025^5 ]^(1/5) − 1 = 2.10%
Shortcut: 2 × 2.30 − 2.50 = 2.10%

The market expects 2.50% inflation a year for 5 years, then 2.10% a year for the 5 years after that. This is the 5y5y forward, the indicator central banks watch the most. It strips out the short term (energy, temporary shocks) and measures whether the market believes inflation will come back to the 2% target over the long run. If it rises clearly above, the central bank has a credibility problem, and it reacts harder.

docs.title: The inflation swap
docs.text:
Desks do not only trade bonds. They use zero-coupon inflation swaps, which give the breakeven without buying or selling a bond, with the same logic as an interest rate swap.

  • The fixed payer pays (1 + K)^T − 1 at maturity (K = the fixed inflation rate, T = years).
  • It receives CPI(T) / CPI(0) − 1, the inflation actually measured.
  • Only the difference is exchanged.

Example. 10 years, K = 2.30%, notional $10m.

Fixed leg:  1.023^10 − 1 = 25.53%
If prices rose 28% in total over 10 years:
  the fixed payer receives 28% − 25.53% = 2.47% of notional = about $247,000
If prices only rose 20%:
  it loses 25.53% − 20% = 5.53% = about $553,000

Banks and pension funds use it. A pension fund that has to pay inflation-linked pensions receives inflation to hedge itself.

docs.title: The trade and its P&L
docs.text:
You think inflation will be above the breakeven. You buy the TIPS and sell a nominal of the same maturity. This is a breakeven trade (long breakevens).

Since the two bonds do not have the same duration, you size with DV01 to keep the same rate sensitivity and keep only the bet on inflation.

Example. Buy $10m of 10-year TIPS (real duration 8.4) and sell 10-year nominal (duration 8.0).

TIPS DV01        = 10,000,000 × 8.4 × 0.0001 = $8,400 per bp
Nominal to sell  = 8,400 / (8.0 × 0.0001) = $10.5m

If the real yield falls 54 bps and the nominal does not move, the breakeven goes from about 2.30% to 2.84%.

P&L ≈ 8,400 × 54 = $453,600

Careful, this calculation assumes the nominal yield is unchanged. In reality, when inflation surprises up, both yields move. The trade only keeps the difference.

docs.title: March 2020, Covid: the breakeven collapses
docs.text:
The US 10-year breakeven (the St. Louis Fed's T10YIE series) went from about 1.7% in early March 2020 to about 0.5% in less than two weeks, with a low around 19 March (secondary sources give 0.50%). It ended the month around 0.87%. Oil collapsed, demand collapsed, and investors were paying almost nothing for inflation protection.

But it was not only a deflation forecast. During the dash for cash in March 2020, investors sold everything sellable, including TIPS, which are less liquid than nominals. The liquidity premium blew out, which crushed the breakeven. Part of the move is noise, not information.

docs.title: 2021-2022: inflation comes back
docs.text:
US inflation went from about 1.4% in early 2021 to above 9% in June 2022. The 10-year breakeven rose to around 3% on 21 April 2022 (2.99% or 3.02% depending on the source), its highest since 2008. Then the Fed hiked (episode 26) and the breakeven fell back to about 2.1% to 2.3% by the end of 2022.

What it shows. The market did not believe inflation would stay at 8-9%. A 10-year breakeven around 3% is not 9%. The 10-year was pricing that the Fed would bring inflation down. Breakevens at 1 or 2 years were much higher (above 4% in spring 2022). The inverted curve of breakevens said the same as the rate curve, inflation now, moderation later.

docs.title: September 2022, UK: linkers in the LDI crisis
docs.text:
The LDI fund crisis of episode 27 also hit index-linked gilts. UK pension funds hold linkers because the pensions they pay are linked to inflation. LDI funds offer leveraged exposure to gilts, including index-linked ones. When forced selling started, the Bank of England first bought conventional long gilts from 28 September, then widened its purchases to index-linked gilts on 11 October 2022, a first for it.

The lesson. Breakevens and linkers are hedging instruments for huge players. When they sell under pressure, prices move a lot, and it has nothing to do with expected inflation.

docs.title: Classic pitfalls
docs.text:
• Taking the breakeven for a pure inflation forecast. It contains a risk premium and a liquidity premium.
  • Comparing different maturities. The 5-year and 10-year breakevens do not measure the same thing. The 5y5y is the right tool for the distant period.
  • Forgetting the index lag. TIPS use the CPI with a lag of about 3 months (interpolated between two months). Principal adjustments therefore lag actual prices.
  • Not sizing the trade. Buying $10m of TIPS and selling $10m of nominal is not rate-neutral, because the durations differ. You have to go through DV01.
  • The deflation floor. In the US, principal is never repaid below the original par. That has value (it is an option), especially for recently issued TIPS.
  • Mixing realised inflation and the change in the breakeven. If realised inflation ends up above the breakeven but the breakeven fell in the meantime, a trade closed before maturity can lose.

docs.title: The S&T interview angle
docs.text:
"What is an inflation breakeven?" The difference between the yield on a nominal bond and on an inflation-linked bond of the same maturity. It is the inflation level where both pay the same. Nominal 4.20%, real 1.90%, breakeven 2.30% (2.26% with Fisher).

"Does that mean the market forecasts 2.30% inflation?" Not exactly. The breakeven also contains an inflation risk premium and a liquidity premium. In March 2020, liquidity made it fall much more than real expectations.

"Your trade if you think inflation will be higher than the market prices?" Long breakeven, buy the TIPS and sell a nominal of the same maturity, sized on DV01. Or receive inflation on a zero-coupon swap.

"What is the 5y5y?" The expected annual inflation rate between 5 years and 10 years from now. Central banks watch it because it measures how well long-term expectations are anchored.

"Who receives inflation on a swap?" Pension funds and insurers with inflation-linked liabilities. They want to be covered if it rises.

"Why does the Fed care?" Because if long-term expectations come loose from 2%, people and companies set wages and prices higher, and inflation feeds itself. The central bank then has to hike harder.

docs.title: Links to previous episodes
docs.text:
• The Policy Rate, the central bank hikes to bring inflation back to target.
  • QE and QT, the UK LDI crisis also hit linkers.
  • Pricing Rate Cuts, same logic of reading an expectation in a price, and the same forward between two horizons.
  • Duration and DV01, to size the breakeven trade.
  • Interest Rate Swaps, the inflation swap has the same structure.
  • FX Forwards, same forward formula between two horizons.

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text:
• An inflation-linked bond adjusts its principal with inflation. Its yield is the real yield.
  • Breakeven ≈ nominal yield − real yield. Exact with Fisher: (1 + nominal) = (1 + real) × (1 + inflation).
  • If inflation ends above the breakeven, the TIPS wins. Otherwise, the nominal wins.
  • The breakeven contains a risk premium and a liquidity premium. It is not a pure forecast.
  • The 5y5y forward, f ≈ 2 × BE10 − BE5, measures how well long-term expectations are anchored.
  • The long-breakeven trade is sized on DV01. March 2020 (0.5%), April 2022 (about 3%) and the UK linker episode show breakevens also move for liquidity reasons.

docs.title: 32. ETFs
docs.text: Episode 32

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: Everyone owns an ETF or knows someone who does. Almost nobody knows why its price stays glued to what it holds. It is an arbitrage story, like put-call parity or the FX forward, with a formula, calculations you can redo by hand, and real cases where the mechanism broke. It is also a classic interview question.

docs.title: What an ETF is
docs.text:
ETF = exchange-traded fund. A fund holds a basket of assets (for example the 500 stocks of the S&P 500) and you buy a share of the fund on the stock exchange, like a stock.

Two prices matter.

  • The NAV (net asset value). What the basket inside is actually worth, per share.
  • The market price. What the ETF trades at on the exchange.
NAV per share = (value of all assets − liabilities) / number of shares

If the basket is worth $5,000,000 and there are 50,000 shares, NAV is $100.

A traditional fund (a mutual fund) is bought and sold at NAV directly from the fund, once a day. An ETF trades between investors all day, so its price could drift away from NAV. It almost doesn't, because of one mechanism.

docs.title: Why the price stays close to NAV
docs.text: Players called authorized participants (APs), big banks and market makers, have the right to create and destroy ETF shares directly with the issuer. It is done in blocks called creation units (for example 50,000 shares, the size varies by fund), usually in kind, meaning the basket is swapped for shares, not cash.

docs.title: The ETF trades above NAV (premium)
docs.text:
NAV $100, market price $100.40.

premium = 100.40 / 100 − 1 = +0.40%

The AP does this.

  1. Buys the basket on the market, 50,000 × $100 = $5,000,000.
  2. Hands it to the issuer, who gives back 50,000 new shares.
  3. Sells them at $100.40, so 50,000 × 100.40 = $5,020,000.
  4. Profit = $20,000 (before costs).

Selling all those shares pushes the ETF price down toward NAV.

docs.title: The ETF trades below NAV (discount)
docs.text:
NAV $100, price $99.60, a discount of −0.40%.

  1. The AP buys 50,000 shares for $4,980,000.
  2. Gives them back to the issuer and receives the basket, worth $5,000,000.
  3. Sells the basket.
  4. Profit = $20,000.

Buying the shares pushes the price up toward NAV.

docs.title: The limit
docs.text:
maximum gap ≈ AP's costs (trading fees + bid-ask + hedging cost)

As long as the gap is bigger than the costs, the arbitrage pays, so someone does it, so the gap closes. This is the arbitrage band.

docs.title: The live price, iNAV
docs.text: The official NAV is calculated once a day, at the close. During the session the issuer publishes an estimate, the iNAV (indicative NAV), recalculated every few seconds from the basket's prices. It is the APs' reference.

docs.title: Primary market and secondary market
docs.text:
Primary market Secondary market Who APs and the issuer All investors What Creating and destroying shares, in blocks Buying and selling existing shares on the exchange Price At NAV (basket against shares) Market price, with a bid-ask

When you buy an ETF on the exchange, you buy an existing share from another investor. The ETF does not need to sell any assets. The primary market only steps in when demand or supply goes beyond what the secondary market absorbs.

docs.title: Tracking difference
docs.text:
tracking difference = ETF return − index return
                    ≈ − expense ratio + securities lending income − trading costs

Example. Index +8.00%, expense ratio 0.20%, the ETF returns +7.82%. The tracking difference is −0.18% (the fund also earned a bit by lending out its securities).

Tracking error is something else. It is the volatility of that gap over time. A low tracking error means the ETF follows the index closely day after day.

docs.title: The effect of fees over 10 years
docs.text:
$10,000 invested for 10 years with a gross return of 7% a year.

Annual fee Value after 10 years 0.20% (index ETF) 10,000 × 1.068^10 = $19,307 1.00% (typical active fund) 10,000 × 1.06^10 = $17,908 Gap $1,398, about 14% of the starting capital

docs.title: The bid-ask
docs.text: When you buy and sell, you also pay the gap between the bid and the ask. For a liquid ETF it can be 0.01% to 0.05%. On $100,000 with a 0.04% bid-ask, a round trip costs about $40. For a thinly traded ETF it can exceed 0.5%.

docs.title: When the mechanism breaks
docs.text: The arbitrage works as long as the AP can buy and sell the basket quickly and at a known price. In a panic, that is no longer true.

docs.title: 1. 24 August 2015, the ETF "flash crash"
docs.text:
On Monday 24 August 2015, the US market opened after a sell-off in Chinese markets. The S&P 500 was down about 5% at one point in the session. Many stocks opened late or were halted repeatedly (individual circuit-breaker rules), so the basket had no reliable price. The iNAV became wrong and APs no longer knew how to arbitrage.

According to the SEC's research note published in December 2015, about 19% of exchange-traded products (ETPs) fell 20% or more at some point in the session, against under 5% of single stocks. More than a thousand halts hit 327 ETPs. Some ETFs traded far below their NAV for a few minutes, because there was no reference price for the stocks they held.

Why. An ETF's price is derived from the basket. With no price for the basket, the ETF price becomes just a panic price, which corrects when the basket starts quoting again.

docs.title: 2. March 2020, bond ETFs
docs.text:
Bonds trade rarely, over the counter (OTC). In a panic, the ETF can be the only thing trading. It becomes the real "price discovery", and the NAV, calculated from stale or estimated bond prices, lags behind.

Numbers from that period.

  • The US bond ETF BND (total bond market) traded about 6% below its NAV on 12 March 2020, then came back to about a 1.7% discount the next day.
  • The corporate bond ETF LQD traded below its NAV by roughly 3% to 5% depending on the measure and the moment, in the week of 16 to 20 March.
  • On 23 March the Fed announced it would buy corporate bond ETFs, a first. Right after, LQD went from a discount of about 2.8% on 20 March to a premium of about 2.9% on 23 March, while its NAV had only gained about 1.4%. ETF purchases only started several weeks later, which shows the announcement was enough.

Why. APs could no longer buy the bond basket, which was barely selling, so they could no longer arbitrage the discount. And the discount was not necessarily an error. It reflected that the real value of the bonds was lower than the displayed NAV.

The lesson. An ETF is only as liquid as its assets. The less liquid the underlying (corporate bonds, high yield, emerging market debt), the bigger the gap to NAV can get under stress.

docs.title: Leveraged ETFs, the effect of daily reset
docs.text:
A 2x ETF aims for 2 times the daily return of the index, not 2 times over a longer period. It resets its leverage every day.

Example. The index rises 10% one day and falls 10% the next.

Index:      1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99      so −1%
2x ETF:     1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96      so −4%

"2 times" would have been −2%. Three days (+10%, −10%, +10%):

Index:      1.10 × 0.90 × 1.10 = 1.089     +8.9%
2x ETF:     1.20 × 0.80 × 1.20 = 1.152     +15.2%   (not +17.8%)

The more the index oscillates, the wider the gap. This "volatility drag" is why these products are meant for a few days, not years.

docs.title: Physical or synthetic replication
docs.text:
• Physical. The ETF actually holds the stocks or bonds of the index (or a representative sample).
  • Synthetic. The ETF holds a different basket and enters a swap with a bank, which pays it the index return. Common in Europe for indices that are hard to access. One extra risk, the bank on the swap (counterparty risk, seen in the CDS episode).

docs.title: Classic pitfalls
docs.text:
• Buying an illiquid ETF at any price. The bid-ask can eat several months of return. Use limit orders and look at the iNAV.
  • Trading at the open or close of a wild session. That is when the gap to NAV is widest.
  • Confusing the ETF's liquidity with its assets' liquidity. A bond ETF trades like a stock but its basket does not.
  • Forgetting volatility drag on leveraged or inverse ETFs.
  • Thinking tracking error is a cost. It is a dispersion, the cost is the tracking difference.
  • Ignoring counterparty risk on synthetic ETFs.
  • Treating a discount as a gift. In March 2020, the discount partly reflected a real value lower than NAV, not only a pricing error.

docs.title: The S&T interview angle
docs.text:
"How does an ETF stay close to its NAV?" Through authorized participant arbitrage. If the ETF trades above NAV, the AP buys the basket, creates shares and sells them, which pushes the price down. Below NAV, it buys shares, redeems them for the basket and sells it, which pushes the price up.

"Why can a bond ETF trade at a much bigger discount than an equity ETF?" Because arbitrage requires being able to buy or sell the basket. Bonds trade rarely and the NAV uses stale prices. Under stress, the ETF becomes the real price.

"What is the difference between tracking error and tracking difference?" Tracking difference is the cumulative return gap between the ETF and its index, roughly the fees. Tracking error is the volatility of that gap.

"Why doesn't a 2x ETF make twice the performance over a year?" It resets its leverage every day. When the market oscillates, compounding loses value. Example, +10% then −10% gives −1% for the index and −4% for the 2x.

"What is a market maker's role on an ETF?" Quote a bid-ask, hedge its risk with the basket or futures, and create or redeem shares when the gap exceeds its costs.

"Can ETF flows move the market?" Yes. Large creations or redemptions force APs to buy or sell the underlying basket, which weighs on its prices, especially for less liquid assets.

docs.text:

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text:
• An ETF is a listed basket. NAV = (assets − liabilities) / number of shares.
  • Its price stays close to NAV because authorized participants create or redeem shares in blocks, and pocket the gap (example, 0.40% on $5m = $20,000).
  • The real cost is tracking difference (≈ expense ratio) plus the bid-ask. 0.20% versus 1.00% in fees is about $1,400 on $10,000 over 10 years.
  • The arbitrage breaks when the basket has no reliable price (24 August 2015) or cannot trade (bonds in March 2020).
  • Leveraged ETFs reset their leverage every day. +10% then −10% gives −1% for the index and −4% for a 2x.
  • An ETF is only as liquid as its assets.

docs.title: 33. Bond Futures
docs.text: Episode 33

docs.title: Why this episode
docs.text: The bond future is the product a rates desk looks at all day. It is the most liquid tool for hedging or betting on rates, it connects directly to repo, DV01 and the carry of episode 29, and it is a classic S&T interview question ("what is the cheapest-to-deliver?"). It has a formula, examples you can redo by hand, and a real case where it broke (March 2020).

docs.title: First, what a future is
docs.text:
A future is a contract to buy or sell something at a fixed price, on a fixed date. Unlike a forward (episode 28), it trades on an exchange and is settled every day.

  • You post a small deposit, the margin.
  • Every evening, the price move is paid in cash. If you are long and the price falls, you pay. If it rises, you receive. This is mark-to-market.

Example. A US 10-year Treasury future, contract size $100,000, price quoted per 100.

Buy 1 contract at 110.00, the price falls to 109.00
loss = (110 − 109) / 100 × 100,000 = $1,000, paid that same day

The price is quoted in points and 32nds of a point. 1/32 of a point is worth 100,000 / 32 / 100 = $31.25. On the 10-year, the smallest quoting step (the tick) is half of that, so $15.625.

docs.title: A bond future
docs.text:
It is a contract to deliver a government bond at a future date. The problem is that a government issues many different bonds, with different coupons and maturities. So the exchange lets the seller choose which one to deliver, from a basket of eligible bonds (for the standard US 10-year, securities with between 6.5 and 10 years of remaining life).

To compare these bonds fairly, each one gets a conversion factor (CF).

CF = price of the bond if it yielded 6%  (per 1 of par)

The 6% is a reference yield set by the exchange, not a coupon.

Example. A 10-year bond with a 4% coupon, valued at a 6% yield.

CF ≈ 0.8512

The lower the coupon, the smaller the CF, because the bond is worth less at 6%.

docs.title: What the seller receives
docs.text:
invoice price = futures price × CF + accrued interest

Accrued interest is the part of the next coupon the seller has already earned.

Example. Future at 110.00, CF = 0.85.

110.00 × 0.85 = 93.50   (+ accrued interest)

docs.title: The cheapest-to-deliver (CTD)
docs.text:
The seller picks the bond that costs the least to buy compared with what they will receive. For each bond in the basket:

net cost = clean price of the bond − futures price × CF

Example. Future at 110.00.

Bond Clean price CF Futures × CF Net cost A 93.80 0.85 93.50 0.30 B 101.90 0.92 101.20 0.70

Bond A has the lowest net cost, so it is the CTD. The futures price follows the CTD bond.

That is why a bond future is not tied to one specific bond. Its price is roughly:

futures price ≈ (CTD price + carry cost) / CF

docs.title: Which bond becomes the CTD
docs.text: The CF is calculated at 6%. When market yields are below 6%, the CTD tends to be the bond with the shortest duration in the basket. When they are above 6%, it tends to be the one with the longest duration. When yields move and a different bond becomes the cheapest, the CTD is said to switch. That changes the future's sensitivity to rates, which matters for hedging.

docs.title: The basis and the implied repo
docs.text:
The basis is the net cost above. It is what you pay to hold the bond rather than the future.

The implied repo rate is the return you earn by buying the CTD and selling the future to deliver it.

implied repo = (invoice price / bond's dirty price today − 1) × 360 / days

Example. CTD A. Dirty price today 94.80 (93.80 clean + 1.00 accrued). Delivery in 90 days, accrued then 2.00, future at 110.00.

invoice price = 110 × 0.85 + 2.00 = 95.50
implied repo = (95.50 / 94.80 − 1) × 360 / 90 = 2.95%

Compare with the real repo rate, what it costs to finance the bond.

Situation Consequence Real repo 4.30% > implied repo 2.95% Borrowing costs more than the trade earns. No trade. The future is expensive versus the bond. Real repo < implied repo Buy the bond (financed in repo), sell the future, pocket the gap almost risk-free. This is the basis trade.

docs.title: Hedging a portfolio with futures
docs.text:
A future's DV01 is roughly the CTD's DV01 divided by its CF.

Example. CTD A has a modified duration of about 7.5, price 93.80.

CTD DV01 per $100,000 of face = 93.80% × 100,000 × 7.5 × 0.0001 = $70.35
DV01 of one futures contract  = 70.35 / 0.85 = $82.76

A bond portfolio has a DV01 of $42,000 per basis point. To hedge it, you sell futures.

contracts to sell = 42,000 / 82.76 ≈ 507

The duration and DV01 figures here are orders of magnitude for the example, not market data.

docs.title: Why hedge funds love the basis
docs.text: The basis trade earns a tiny gap. So funds run it with huge leverage, financing the bond purchase in repo. It is carry (episode 29): a small steady gain, a big loss if it unwinds.

docs.title: March 2020
docs.text:
In early March 2020 the Treasury market tightened. Basis trade positions suffered losses and margin calls (on both futures and repo). Funds sold the bonds they held and bought back futures. One analysis puts the reduction in hedge funds' short futures positions at roughly $62bn between 3 and 17 March 2020, matched by an unwind of repo-financed bond positions.

That unwind pushed yields up and widened the basis, which hurt other funds. The Fed bought Treasuries in huge size, often cited at about $1.6tn between March and May 2020 (secondary source).

A nuance. Researchers disagree on how much the basis trade mattered. The OFR and the Dallas Fed say the unwind amplified the stress. A Cleveland Fed study argues it was more a consequence than a main cause. The safe point is that the positions were leveraged, and the unwind happened at the same time as the rest of the crisis.

docs.title: Classic pitfalls
docs.text:
• Thinking a future tracks a single bond. It tracks the CTD, which can change.
  • Forgetting the conversion factor. DV01 and hedging are calculated with the CF.
  • Confusing future and forward. A future is settled daily (margin calls), a forward at maturity.
  • The 6% is not a coupon. It is a reference yield used to calculate the CF.
  • Ignoring mark-to-market. A position that is winning on paper can drain cash if margin calls hit before the price comes back.
  • Treating the basis trade as riskless. Without leverage it is almost riskless. With leverage of 50 or 100, it is a short position on funding volatility.
  • Using rough duration figures to hedge. The CTD's DV01 has to be recalculated when yields move.

docs.title: The S&T interview angle
docs.text:
"What is the cheapest-to-deliver?" The bond in the eligible basket that the future's seller has the most interest in delivering, the one that minimises bond price minus futures price times conversion factor. The futures price follows the CTD.

"What is the conversion factor for?" To make bonds with different coupons and maturities comparable. It is the price of the bond at a 6% yield, per unit of par.

"How do you hedge a portfolio with futures?" I calculate the portfolio's DV01, the DV01 of one contract (the CTD's DV01 divided by its CF), and sell the number of contracts that equalises the two.

"What is a basis trade?" Buy the CTD bond financed in repo and sell the future. I earn the implied repo minus the real repo cost. A small gain, scaled up with a lot of leverage.

"What happened in March 2020?" Leveraged basis trades took margin calls during the liquidity crisis, sold their bonds, pushed yields up, and the Fed had to buy Treasuries in huge size.

"When does the CTD switch?" When yields move enough for another bond in the basket to become the cheapest to deliver. Below 6% yield, it tends to be the shortest duration.

docs.text:

docs.title: Key takeaway
docs.text:
• A future is a standardised contract, settled daily (mark-to-market, margin).
  • A bond future lets the seller choose which bond to deliver from a basket. Invoice price = futures price × CF + accrued interest.
  • The CTD is the bond that minimises: price − future × CF. The future follows the CTD.
  • Implied repo = (invoice / dirty price − 1) × 360 / days. If it is above the real repo, the basis trade pays.
  • DV01 of one contract ≈ CTD DV01 / CF. It is used to size a hedge.
  • The basis trade is leveraged carry, and it unwound in March 2020, with the Fed having to buy Treasuries in huge size.
